  storage as the React AppShell (`uiset-sidebar`), and each link then gets a tooltip.
  Below `narrow-below` (48rem by default) the sidebar moves into a drawer opened from the
  header.
- `<uiset-page-header title description level>` is the page's `h1` (or `h2`) with your
  actions as children. `<uiset-empty-state title description icon level>` says what to do
  when there's nothing yet, with its actions as children. On both, `title` names the page
  or state; it isn't a tooltip.

## Content and forms

The web twins of React's `table`, `avatar-group`, `CountBadge`, `code-block`,
`inline-edit`, `upload`, `schema-form`, `sortable-list` and `sortable-tree`. `web/content.html` has each
of them.

```html
<uiset-table label="Invoices" stack sticky-header sticky-column max-height="20rem">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>Invoice</th><th>Customer</th><th data-align="end">Amount</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody><tr><th scope="row">INV-001</th><td>Acme Corp</td><td data-align="end">$2,500</td></tr></tbody>
  </table>
</uiset-table>

<uiset-avatar-group label="Reviewers" max="3">
  <ui-avatar><ui-avatar-fallback>AL</ui-avatar-fallback></ui-avatar>
  …
</uiset-avatar-group>

<uiset-count-badge count="3" label="3 unread">
  <ui-button><button type="button" data-variant="outline">Inbox</button></ui-button>
</uiset-count-badge>

<uiset-code-block language="tsx" caption="app.tsx" line-numbers highlight="3"></uiset-code-block>
<uiset-package-command install="@uiset/web @ui-sdk/web"></uiset-package-command>
<uiset-code-tabs label="Framework"></uiset-code-tabs>

<uiset-inline-edit label="Project name" value="Atlas" actions></uiset-inline-edit>
<uiset-upload label="Attachments" hint="PNG, JPG or PDF, up to 5 MB each" accept="image/*,.pdf" max-size="5000000"></uiset-upload>
<uiset-schema-form confirm="Sends an invite email to the address given" done-message="Invite sent."></uiset-schema-form>
<uiset-sortable-list label="Playlist" multiple></uiset-sortable-list>
<uiset-sortable-tree label="Pages" icons></uiset-sortable-tree>
```

```ts
code.code = source // or the text inside the element
tabs.items = [{ value: "vue", label: "Vue", language: "vue", code: "…" }, …]
project.validate = (text) => (text.trim() ? null : "Give the project a name.")
project.addEventListener("valuechange", (e) => rename(e.detail.value)) // preventDefault() refuses
files.upload = (file, { signal, onProgress }) => send(file, signal, onProgress) // returns a Promise
files.addEventListener("uploaded", (e) => attach(e.detail.result))
invite.form = defineForm({ name: "invite_teammate", title: "Invite a teammate", fields: { … } })
invite.send = async (values) => (await sendInvite(values)).problems // shown under their fields
playlist.items = [{ value: "intro", label: "Intro", locked: true }, { value: "harbor", label: "Harbor Lights" }]
playlist.addEventListener("valuechange", (e) => save(e.detail.value)) // the keys in their new order
pages.items = [{ value: "guides", label: "Guides", children: [] }, { value: "faq", label: "FAQ" }]
pages.addEventListener("itemschange", (e) => save(e.detail.value)) // the items, nested again
```

- `<uiset-table>` puts your `<table>` in a scroll area named by `label`. With `stack`, below
  30rem of its own width each row becomes a block of labelled values: each cell is labelled
  by its column's heading, and the parts state their table roles, which browsers drop when
  CSS changes a table's display. A cell's own `data-label` stays. `data-align="end"` aligns a
  column. Rows added later are labelled too, and a framework can add and remove the table
  where it put it.
- `<uiset-avatar-group>` shows `max` avatars, then a count of the rest, named in words ("2
  more"; `more-label` with `{count}` words it). `total` counts avatars you didn't render.
- `<uiset-count-badge>` shows `count`, "99+" past `max`, a dot with `dot`, and nothing at 0
  unless `show-zero`. `label` is what screen readers and agents hear, so say what's counted.
- `<uiset-code-block>` colors code with shiki, when it's on the page, as the chat does. The
  caption is `caption` (the language without one); `copy="false"` leaves out the copy
  button, which is named for the caption ("Copy app.tsx"). `wrap` wraps long lines.
- `<uiset-package-command>` takes `install` (with `dev`) or `run`. The choice of package
  manager is one for every command on the page, React's included, and kept for the next
  visit. `<uiset-code-tabs>` is the same tabs for any `items`; its `value` is the tab showing.
- `<uiset-inline-edit>` is React's `InlineEdit` on the same primitive: a press, Enter or F2
  edits, Enter or leaving saves, Escape cancels, and text `validate` refuses stays in the
  field with the problem. `actions` adds Save and Cancel for touch. Agents call `setValue`,
  `startEditing` and `cancel` by its label.
- `<uiset-upload>` is UI SDK's file input with the upload queue: files go up `concurrency`
  at a time (3), each row shows a preview, its size, status and progress, with Cancel, Retry
  and Remove, and files that fail `accept`, `max-size` or `max-files` are listed with why.
  The list is one tab stop: Enter on a row that stopped retries it, Delete removes it. It
  fires `valuechange`, `itemschange`, `uploaded`, `failed` and `reject`; `labels` and
  `messages` word it.
- `<uiset-schema-form>` is React's `SchemaForm` on the same primitive: set `form` to what
  `defineForm` returns (exported from `@uiset/web`) and `send` to what sends the values;
  problems it returns show under their fields. It draws UI SDK's own fields, steps and a
  review; `value` is live for `v-model`, and agents fill it by field name or label while a
  person presses the submit. See [Forms](./forms.md#web-components).
- `<uiset-sortable-list>` is React's `SortableList` on the same primitive: set `items`, and
  drag an item or pick it up with Space. `multiple` lets a selection move together, an item
  with `locked` stays put, and `numbered` shows places. `value` (the order) and `selected` are
  live; it fires `valuechange` and `selectedchange`, and agents call `moveItem` and
  `selectItems` by its label. See [Sortable lists and trees](./lists.md#web-components).
- `<uiset-sortable-tree>` is React's `SortableTree` on the same primitive: set nested `items`
  and drag a row up, down and sideways, or press Space and use the arrows. Only branches
  hold items; a drop elsewhere goes back and says why. `items` and `expanded` are live; it
  fires `itemschange`, `expandedchange` and `action`, and agents call `moveItem`,
  `expandItem` and `collapseItem` by its label.

### Confirm button

`<uiset-confirm-button>` is for something hard to undo: the first press arms it and says
`confirm-label`, the second fires `confirm` with `{ source, waitUntil }`. Escape, leaving it
or `timeout` (4000 ms) disarms it, and a second press within 600 ms doesn't count. `confirm`
tells agents what it does: the bridge asks the person first, and an approved press acts.

```html
<uiset-confirm-button confirm="Deletes the Atlas project" confirm-label="Press again to delete">
  Delete project
</uiset-confirm-button>
```

### Radio cards

React's `RadioCard` is UI SDK's own elements in UISet's classes: each card is a `ui-field`,
so its radio is named by the title alone and described by the line under it, and a press
anywhere on the card chooses it. `web/index.html` has a set.

```html
<ui-field>
  <ui-field-label>Plan</ui-field-label>
  <ui-radio-group class="uiset-radio-cards" default-value="pro">
    <ui-field class="uiset-radio-card">
      <ui-radio value="pro"><ui-radio-indicator></ui-radio-indicator></ui-radio>
      <span class="uiset-radio-card-text">
        <ui-field-label>Pro</ui-field-label>
        <ui-field-description>Per month, for growing teams.</ui-field-description>
      </span>
      <span class="uiset-radio-card-aside">$20</span>
    </ui-field>
  </ui-radio-group>
</ui-field>
```

### A textarea's count

`<uiset-textarea-count>` counts its field's textarea against the limit as people type. In the
field's description, a screen reader hears it with the textarea; near the limit it says how
many are left, once at `warn-at` (20) and once at none. With no `max` it takes the textarea's
`maxlength`; `messages` translates its words.

```html
<ui-field>
  <ui-field-label>Release notes</ui-field-label>
  <ui-textarea><textarea maxlength="160"></textarea></ui-textarea>
  <ui-field-description class="uiset-textarea-count">
    <uiset-textarea-count max="160"></uiset-textarea-count>
  </ui-field-description>
</ui-field>
```

### Password rules

`<uiset-password-rules>` lists the rules a new password has to meet as `<li>` children, each
with `data-min-length`, `data-pattern` (a regular expression) or both. It reads its field's
password input as people type, ticks off each rule, says "Done" or "To do" to screen readers,
and announces a rule that changes, once. `label` names the list ("Password rules").

```html
<ui-field>
  <ui-field-label>Create a password</ui-field-label>
  <ui-password-input>
    <input autocomplete="new-password" />
    <ui-password-input-toggle><button aria-label="Show password"></button></ui-password-input-toggle>
  </ui-password-input>
  <uiset-password-rules>
    <li data-min-length="12">At least 12 characters</li>
    <li data-pattern="\d">A number</li>
  </uiset-password-rules>
</ui-field>
```

### Rings

`data-shape="ring"` on a `ui-meter` or `ui-progress` draws it as a ring filled to its value,
with `ui-meter-value` in the middle and `ui-meter-label` under it. A `ui-progress` with no
value turns a quarter of its ring, held still for reduced motion.

```html
<ui-meter data-shape="ring" value="62">
  <ui-meter-value></ui-meter-value>
  <ui-meter-label>Reading goal</ui-meter-label>
</ui-meter>
```

### Scroll areas

A `ui-scroll-area` fades where its content runs on past an edge. `data-fades="none"` on it
turns that off, and `--uiset-fade` sets how far the fade reaches. `data-frame="none"` drops
its border and padding, for one inside a larger surface, and it fills the space it's given.

The kits and templates scroll in UI SDK's scroll areas too: the chat thread, the terminal,
the data grid, the schedule, the board, the chart's table, the IDE's files, tabs and code, the
rich text editor and the agent snapshot. Each one's old scrolling class (like
`chat-thread-scroller` or `data-grid-scroller`) is on the viewport, the element that scrolls.
Two keep the browser's own scrolling, since what's inside them is your own markup:
`<uiset-status-bar>` and `<uiset-pull-refresh>`.

## Page templates

Every React page template is a web page too, in `web/templates/`, built only from UI SDK's
elements and UISet's. Each one's sample data is a framework-free module the React template
imports as well (`registry/uiset/ui/templates/*-sample.ts`), so the two show the same thing.

| Page | What it shows |
| ---- | ------------- |
| `auth.html` | Sign in, sign up, forgot and reset password, verify a code: browser checks, server messages, a strength meter |
| `pricing.html` | Plans with a monthly or yearly switch, a comparison table and questions |
| `dashboard.html` | A date range that rescopes the figures, charts and recent orders, in the App Shell |
| `admin.html` | Records with search, filters and export; create and edit in a drawer; confirmed bulk delete |
| `settings.html` | Profile, security, notifications, billing with usage and invoices, team, and a danger zone |
| `inbox.html` | Folders, a message list you arrow through, the message with star, archive, delete and Undo, and compose |
| `chat-app.html` | Chats, the conversation and a composer with a model picker and usage, streaming from a stand-in model |
| `project-board.html` | Sprint progress and the issues as a board or a list, with search, a person filter, card details, a new-issue form and Undo |
| `calendar-app.html` | A day, a week (`uiset-schedule`) or a month (`uiset-schedule-month`), a small month that jumps to a day, calendars to show or hide, and what's next |
| `../ide.html` | The IDE in resizable panes |

The chat app streams from `sampleAssistant` (`templates/chat-app-sample.ts`), an async
generator of events (text, reasoning, tool calls, sources). Swap in your model there; the
page turns its events into the chat's message parts, the same shape AI SDK's `useChat`
holds, so `useChat`'s `messages` and `status` can go into `<uiset-chat>` directly instead.

## Server-rendered HTML

A framework that hydrates expects the HTML it rendered on the server, and UISet's elements
draw themselves as they're defined. Mark the container the framework hydrates with
`data-uiset-hydrating`: the elements under it are defined, so the framework sets their data
as properties, but they wait to draw until the attribute goes. Remove it once hydration is
done:

```html
<div id="app" data-uiset-hydrating><!-- the server's HTML --></div>
```

```ts
import "@uiset/web"

hydrate() // your framework's
document.getElementById("app")!.removeAttribute("data-uiset-hydrating")
```

`<uiset-root>` doesn't wait, so the skin is there from the start. The module imports on a
server and defines nothing there.

## Vue, Svelte and Solid

[Vue](./vue.md) and [Svelte](./svelte.md) each have a guide: setup, passing arrays and
objects, events, two-way binding, skins, server rendering, and using UI SDK's own Vue and
Svelte components under UISet's stylesheet. Every code block in them ran in a real app.

Solid renders custom elements as they are; listen with `on:valuechange`. UI SDK's Solid
adapter works with `uiset.css` too, since the same `data-slot` attributes mean the same
styles.

## React and the web

Every kit is an element set, and every page template is a web page: Studio, Mobile, Board,
Scheduler, Canvas, the IDE, the Agent Console, the Terminal, Charts with the sparkline and
stat, the Data Grid, Chat and the App Shell, and the auth, pricing, dashboard, admin,
settings, inbox, chat app and IDE pages. The rest of the registry wraps UI SDK's own
components, which are already elements here (`ui-*`, dressed by `uiset.css`); UISet's
pieces without behavior (badge, alert, card, item and description lists, breadcrumbs,
skeleton, spinner, kbd) are classes in the same stylesheet.

The three small parts with behavior of their own are elements too:

```html
<uiset-search-field label="Search mail" placeholder="Search mail…" shortcut="/"></uiset-search-field>
<uiset-copy-button value="npm i @uiset/web" label="Copy" copied-label="Copied"></uiset-copy-button>
<uiset-stepper label="Setup progress" value="details"></uiset-stepper>
```

- `<uiset-search-field>` fires `valuechange` with `{ value }`; `shortcut` ("/" by default,
  `shortcut=""` for none) focuses it from anywhere, through UI SDK's shared shortcuts, and
  shows as a key hint until something is typed. Clear empties it and keeps focus, and
  fires `input` on the field's input as typing does, so a two-way binding follows it.
- `<uiset-copy-button>` copies `value`, announces "Copied" and shows it for a moment, or
  "Couldn't copy" when the browser refuses. `full-label` is a fuller name where several share
  a page, like "Copy app.tsx"; start it with the visible label.
- `<uiset-stepper>` takes `steps` (`{ value, label, description? }`) and `value`; choosing a
  step sets `value` and fires `valuechange`. With `linear` (on unless `linear="false"`),
  later steps wait until the current one is reached.

## Tests

`tests/e2e/web/` runs against plain HTML with no React on the page: axe in every skin
and both themes, the root's attributes, skins restyling UI SDK's elements, the knob and
swipe rows by keyboard, the patch bay by keyboard, by script and by an agent, the Studio
instruments, a UI SDK dialog's focus, and the built files themselves (the module in a
browser and in Node, the stylesheet's reach, and the type declarations).
`frameworks.spec.ts` does by hand what Vue and Svelte do to custom elements: attributes set
as properties, `"false"` for a false binding, lists as text, and children added after an
element mounts. Two unit tests guard the rest: no element may have a member that hides one
of its attributes, and every element the build defines must be in the types. `mobile.spec.ts`,
`board.spec.ts`, `scheduler.spec.ts`, `canvas.spec.ts`, `ide.spec.ts`,
`agent-console.spec.ts`, `terminal.spec.ts`, `charts.spec.ts`, `data-grid.spec.ts` and
`chat.spec.ts` cover those kits' pages, and `templates.spec.ts` the page templates (`web/mobile.html`, `web/board.html`,
`web/schedule.html`, `web/canvas.html`, `web/ide.html`, `web/agent.html`,
`web/terminal.html`, `web/charts.html`, `web/data-grid.html`, `web/chat.html`) the same way: axe in all six skin and theme pairs,
keyboard, pointer, events, script and agents.


<!-- docs/vue.md -->

# Vue

UISet works in Vue 3 through its Web Components build, `@uiset/web`: one module that
defines the `<uiset-*>` elements and one stylesheet with every skin. It's built on UI SDK,
whose own `<ui-*>` elements it dresses. This page covers what is specific to Vue: setup,
passing data, events, skins, UI SDK's Vue components and server rendering. Every element's
attributes, properties and events are in [Web Components](./web-components.md).

This page describes `@uiset/web` 0.3.0 or later.

## Install

```bash
npm install @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web
```

With npm this resolves `@ui-sdk/web` and `@ui-sdk/core` to `0.1.0-beta.10`, the exact
version UISet pins. pnpm takes UI SDK's `latest` tag, the same beta today, which moves on with
UI SDK's next one, so name the versions:

```bash
pnpm add @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web@0.1.0-beta.10 @ui-sdk/core@0.1.0-beta.10
```

`shiki` is optional: with it, code in chats is colored; without it the app still builds and
code blocks are plain.

## Tell Vue the tags are elements

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import vue from "@vitejs/plugin-vue"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    vue({
      template: {
        compilerOptions: {
          isCustomElement: (tag) => tag.startsWith("ui-") || tag.startsWith("uiset-"),
        },
      },
    }),
  ],
})
```

Without it the elements still render, and Vue warns "Failed to resolve component" for each
tag in development.

## A first screen

Import the UI SDK elements you use, then UISet's module and stylesheet, before the app
mounts. `uiset.css` already includes UI SDK's own styles.

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { createApp } from "vue"
import "@ui-sdk/web/button"
import "@ui-sdk/web/dialog"
import "@ui-sdk/web/select"
import "@ui-sdk/web/switch"
import "@uiset/web"
import "@uiset/web/uiset.css"
import App from "./App.vue"

createApp(App).mount("#app")
```

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from "vue"

const steps = [
  { value: "account", label: "Account" },
  { value: "details", label: "Details" },
  { value: "review", label: "Review" },
]
const step = ref("details")
const emails = ref(false)
</script>

<template>
  <uiset-root skin="base">
    <ui-button><button>Save</button></ui-button>
    <ui-button><button data-variant="outline">Cancel</button></ui-button>

    <label>
      <ui-switch @checkedchange="emails = $event.detail.value">
        <ui-switch-thumb></ui-switch-thumb>
      </ui-switch>
      Email me
    </label>

    <uiset-stepper
      label="Setup progress"
      :steps="steps"
      :value="step"
      @valuechange="step = $event.detail.value"
    ></uiset-stepper>

    <uiset-stat
      label="Revenue"
      value="$48,200"
      change="12%"
      direction="up"
      period="vs last month"
    ></uiset-stat>

    <p>Step: {{ step }}. Emails: {{ emails ? "on" : "off" }}.</p>
  </uiset-root>
</template>
```

`<uiset-root>` holds the skin; everything inside takes it.

## Data in

Vue sets a DOM property when the element has one by that name, and an attribute otherwise.
So text goes in as a plain attribute, and arrays, objects and functions go in with an
ordinary `:` binding, as long as the elements are defined before Vue renders (the imports
in `main.ts` above see to that).

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import type { UISetDataGridEvents } from "@uiset/web"
import { ref, shallowRef } from "vue"
import { orders, type Order } from "./data"

const rows = shallowRef<Order[]>(orders)
const columns = [
  { id: "customer", header: "Customer", value: (o: Order) => o.customer, editable: true },
  { id: "plan", header: "Plan", value: (o: Order) => o.plan, options: ["Free", "Pro", "Team"] },
  { id: "seats", header: "Seats", type: "number", value: (o: Order) => o.seats, editable: true },
]
const getRowId = (o: Order) => o.id

const query = ref("")
const selected = ref<string[]>([])

type CellEdit = UISetDataGridEvents<Order>["celledit"]

function onCellEdit(event: CellEdit) {
  const { rowId, column, value } = event.detail
  if (column === "seats" && Number(value) < 1) return event.preventDefault()
  rows.value = rows.value.map((o) => (o.id === rowId ? { ...o, [column]: value } : o))
}

function addOrder() {
  const id = `o${rows.value.length + 1}`
  rows.value = [...rows.value, { id, customer: "New customer", plan: "Free", seats: 1 }]
}
</script>

<template>
  <uiset-search-field
    label="Search orders"
    placeholder="Search orders…"
    :value="query"
    @valuechange="query = $event.detail.value"
  ></uiset-search-field>

  <uiset-data-grid
    label="Orders"
    selectable
    editable
    height="16rem"
    :rows="rows"
    :columns="columns"
    :getRowId="getRowId"
    :query="query"
    :selected="selected"
    @selectedchange="selected = $event.detail.value"
    @celledit="onCellEdit"
  ></uiset-data-grid>
</template>
```

Functions are properties too. A chart takes its data and the functions that read it:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, shallowRef } from "vue"
import { months, type Month } from "./data"

const data = shallowRef<Month[]>(months)
const x = (d: Month) => d.month
const series = [
  { key: "revenue", label: "Revenue", value: (d: Month) => d.revenue },
  { key: "costs", label: "Costs", value: (d: Month) => d.costs },
]
const format = (n: number) => `$${n / 1000}k`
const pinned = ref<string | null>(null)
</script>

<template>
  <uiset-line-chart
    label="Revenue"
    description="By month"
    :data="data"
    :x="x"
    :series="series"
    :format="format"
    :selected="pinned"
    @select="pinned = $event.detail.value"
  ></uiset-line-chart>
  <uiset-sparkline label="Revenue, five months" :values="data.map((d) => d.revenue)"></uiset-sparkline>
</template>
```

Four things to know:

- **Replace arrays, don't change them in place.** An element redraws when its property is
  set again. `rows.value.push(…)` on a deep `ref` changes your state and leaves the grid
  as it was; `rows.value = [...rows.value, row]` redraws it. `shallowRef` fits: the
  element gets your plain array, and only replacing it counts as a change.
- **If Vue renders before the elements are defined**, it finds no property and writes
  `rows="[object Object],…"` as an attribute. Define them first; a server-rendered page
  does that with `data-uiset-hydrating` (see [Server rendering](#server-rendering)).
- **An attribute that turns something on** (`selectable`, `editable`, `toolbar`, the
  root's `sound`) is written bare, as above, or bound to a boolean. `false` turns it off:

```vue
<uiset-data-grid :toolbar="flags.toolbar"></uiset-data-grid>
```

- **A list can be text or an array.** A sparkline's `values` and a stat's `trend` take
  either; an empty place in the text is a gap:

```vue
<uiset-sparkline label="Trend" values="4,6,,8"></uiset-sparkline>
<uiset-sparkline label="Trend" :values="[4, 6, null, 8]"></uiset-sparkline>
<uiset-stat label="Revenue" value="$48,200" trend="31,35,33,40,48"></uiset-stat>
```

The grid's and search field's plain `label`, the boolean bindings and the text lists need
`@uiset/web` 0.3.0 or later.

## Events out

The elements report changes as DOM events, named in lowercase, with the new value in
`event.detail`. Listen with `@`:

| Element                | Event            | `$event.detail`                                   |
| ---------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `<ui-switch>`          | `checkedchange`  | `value`: on or off                                |
| `<ui-select>`          | `valuechange`    | `value`: the chosen item's value                  |
| `<uiset-stepper>`      | `valuechange`    | `value`: the step                                 |
| `<uiset-search-field>` | `valuechange`    | `value`: the text                                 |
| `<uiset-data-grid>`    | `selectedchange` | `value`: the selected row ids                     |
| `<uiset-data-grid>`    | `celledit`       | `rowId`, `column`, `value`; `preventDefault()` refuses the edit |
| `<uiset-line-chart>`   | `select`         | `value`: the pinned position's key, or `null`     |
| `<uiset-patch-bay>`    | `valuechange`    | `value`: the cables, `[{ from, to }]`             |
| `<uiset-knob>`         | `valuechange`    | `value`: a number                                 |

Setting a property fires no event, like a native input, so writing state back into an
element never loops. `$event` is untyped in a template; type the handler's parameter with
the element's event map, as `onCellEdit` does above.

## Two-way binding

`v-model` works on every element with a value a person changes (0.3.0 or later): the
search field, stepper, knob, patch bay, wheel, rich text, code editor, chat composer, chat
threads, model picker, file tree and editor tabs. Vue treats a custom element like a text
input: it sets `value` and reads it back on `input`, and each of these fires `input` once a
change is in.

```vue
<uiset-search-field label="Search orders" v-model="query"></uiset-search-field>
<uiset-stepper label="Setup" :steps="steps" v-model="step"></uiset-stepper>

<span id="level-label">Level</span>
<uiset-knob aria-labelledby="level-label" v-model="level">
  <uiset-knob-indicator></uiset-knob-indicator>
  <uiset-knob-value></uiset-knob-value>
</uiset-knob>

<uiset-patch-bay aria-label="Patch bay" v-model="cables">
  <uiset-patch-bay-jack v-for="jack in jacks" :key="jack.port" :value="jack.port">
    <button :aria-label="jack.name"></button>
  </uiset-patch-bay-jack>
</uiset-patch-bay>
```

- **State set in Vue reaches the element**, and fires nothing, so it never loops.
- **A refused change stays refused.** A `valuechange` listener that calls
  `preventDefault()` keeps the value, and no `input` fires.
- **`v-model.lazy` waits for `change`**: a finished choice, or a knob let go.
- **It doesn't compile for the server.** Vue's server compiler allows `v-model` on
  `<input>`, `<textarea>` and `<select>` only. A server-rendered app binds the value and
  listens, which works on every element:

```vue
<uiset-knob aria-labelledby="level-label" :value="level" @valuechange="level = $event.detail.value">
  <uiset-knob-indicator></uiset-knob-indicator>
  <uiset-knob-value></uiset-knob-value>
</uiset-knob>
```

The same pair works for `:checked` and `@checkedchange` on `<ui-switch>`, `:value` and
`@valuechange` on `<ui-select>`, `:selected` and `@selectedchange` on the grid, and
`:selected` and `@select` on a chart.

## Children

- **Elements that keep your children**: the root, `<ui-button>` around its button, a
  patch bay around its jacks. `v-for` and `v-if` work inside them; a jack added from state
  joins the bay.
- **Elements that draw themselves** (the grid, charts, the stepper, the search field, the
  stat): give them no children.
- **The app shell moves its children** into its sidebar, header and main area. They keep
  updating there, and `v-if` works inside them and straight under the shell: a child that
  appears later is placed in the main area after the others, and leaves again (0.3.0 or
  later).

## The element from script

A template ref is the element, with the properties and methods
[Web Components](./web-components.md) lists. The package exports a type for each element:

```ts
import { iconElement, type UISetDataGrid } from "@uiset/web"

const grid = useTemplateRef<UISetDataGrid>("grid")
const counted = ref(0)
function count() {
  counted.value = grid.value?.rows.length ?? -1
}

const iconHost = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>("icon")
onMounted(() => iconHost.value?.append(iconElement("check")))
```

## TypeScript

- **The package ships its types** (0.3.0 or later): the functions it exports, a type for
  each element with options of its own (`UISetDataGrid`, `UISetStepper`, `UISetPatchBay`
  and the rest; charts and the grid take your row type, as in `UISetLineChart<Month>` and
  `UISetDataGrid<Order>`), and entries in
  `HTMLElementTagNameMap`, so `document.querySelector("uiset-data-grid")` is typed. UI
  SDK's elements are typed the same way once you import them.
- **Templates need nothing by default.** `vue-tsc` accepts the tags with the settings of
  Vite's `vue-ts` template: an unknown tag is unchecked.
- **`strictTemplates` needs the tags declared.** It reports each unknown tag, and each
  `data-` attribute, as an error. The element types describe the elements, not what a
  template may write on them (attributes, properties and listeners together), so the
  declaration names the tags and leaves their options unchecked:

```ts
// src/custom-elements.d.ts
import type { DefineComponent } from "vue"

// Any attribute, property or listener: the tags are known, their options are not checked.
type CustomElement = DefineComponent<Record<string, unknown>>

declare module "vue" {
  interface GlobalComponents {
    [tag: `ui-${string}`]: CustomElement
    [tag: `uiset-${string}`]: CustomElement
  }
}
```

```json
"vueCompilerOptions": { "strictTemplates": true, "dataAttributes": ["data-*"] }
```

- **Events are typed in script.** `grid.addEventListener("celledit", (e) => …)` knows
  `e.detail`. A template's `$event` isn't; name a handler's parameter by the element's
  event map, exported with the elements: `UISetDataGridEvents<Order>["celledit"]`,
  `UISetKnobEvents["valuechange"]`, as `onCellEdit` does.

## Skins and themes

The root's attributes are ordinary bindings, and changing them restyles everything inside
at once. See [Theming](./theming.md) for the skins and their variables.

```vue
<uiset-root :skin="skin" :theme="theme" :sound="sound">
```

| Attribute | Values                                                                      |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `skin`    | `"base"`, `"blueprint"`, `"studio"`, `"phosphor"` or `"ink"`                |
| `theme`   | `"light"` or `"dark"`; `null` removes it and the page follows the system    |
| `sound`   | `true` for interaction sounds, `false` for none (0.3.0 or later)            |

The themed skins have one scheme each (Studio is dark, Ink is light), so, as
[Theming](./theming.md#skins) says, `theme` is for the base skin.

### The key color

`<uiset-root>` has no key color attribute. Set what the React root sets: `data-key` and
three variables, the color's OKLCH lightness, chroma and hue.

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, ref } from "vue"

const key = ref({ l: 0.55, c: 0.2, h: 150 })
const keyStyle = computed(() => ({
  "--uiset-key-l": key.value.l,
  "--uiset-key-c": key.value.c,
  "--uiset-key-h": key.value.h,
}))
</script>

<template>
  <uiset-root skin="base" data-key :style="keyStyle">
    <ui-button><button>Green key</button></ui-button>
  </uiset-root>
</template>
```

### One skin inside another

The nearest root wins, so a root inside a root gives a panel its own skin or theme. It is
only as tall as what's in it (0.3.0 or later).

```vue
<uiset-root :skin="skin" :theme="theme">
  <uiset-root skin="blueprint">
    <ui-button><button>Blueprint</button></ui-button>
  </uiset-root>

  <uiset-root skin="base" theme="light">
    <ui-button><button>Always light</button></ui-button>
  </uiset-root>
</uiset-root>
```

### Fonts

The base skin uses your app's own font: the root and its controls inherit it (0.3.0 or
later). Each themed skin names its faces and falls back to system fonts. Load the ones you
use, for example Studio's from Google Fonts in `index.html`:

```html
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Saira+Semi+Condensed:wght@400;500;600&display=swap"
/>
```

The faces for each skin are listed in [Installation](./installation.md#fonts).

## UI SDK's Vue components with UISet's look

UI SDK also ships native Vue components, `@ui-sdk/vue`. They work with UISet's stylesheet:
they render the same parts with the same `data-slot` and state attributes, and `uiset.css`
styles those attributes. Install the version UISet pins:

```bash
npm install @ui-sdk/vue@0.1.0-beta.10
```

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Button } from "@ui-sdk/vue/button"
import {
  Dialog,
  DialogBackdrop,
  DialogClose,
  DialogContent,
  DialogDescription,
  DialogTitle,
  DialogTrigger,
} from "@ui-sdk/vue/dialog"
import {
  Select,
  SelectContent,
  SelectItem,
  SelectLabel,
  SelectTrigger,
  SelectValue,
} from "@ui-sdk/vue/select"
import { Switch, SwitchThumb } from "@ui-sdk/vue/switch"
import { ref } from "vue"

const emails = ref(false)
const role = ref<string | null>(null)
</script>

<template>
  <uiset-root skin="studio">
    <Button data-variant="solid">Save</Button>
    <Button data-variant="outline">Cancel</Button>
    <label>
      <Switch v-model="emails"><SwitchThumb /></Switch>
      Email me
    </label>
    <Select v-model="role" placeholder="Select a role">
      <SelectLabel>Role</SelectLabel>
      <SelectTrigger><SelectValue /></SelectTrigger>
      <SelectContent>
        <SelectItem value="viewer">Viewer</SelectItem>
        <SelectItem value="editor">Editor</SelectItem>
      </SelectContent>
    </Select>
    <Dialog>
      <DialogTrigger>Share</DialogTrigger>
      <DialogBackdrop />
      <DialogContent>
        <DialogTitle>Share link</DialogTitle>
        <DialogDescription>Anyone with the link can view this.</DialogDescription>
        <DialogClose>Done</DialogClose>
      </DialogContent>
    </Dialog>
  </uiset-root>
</template>
```

What was compared, in the base and Studio skins: the button (solid, outline and with
keyboard focus), the switch (off and on), the select (label, trigger, value, open list and
items) and the dialog (trigger, content, title, description, close and backdrop), each
beside the same control written with the custom elements.

- **The look is the same.** Every computed style on every part matched, apart from what a
  browser gives a tag before any stylesheet: the native switch is a `<button>`, with a
  button's text color and alignment, which a switch doesn't draw with. Screenshots of the
  buttons, the switch, the select's label and trigger, and the open dialog matched.
- **`v-model` works** on the native components, as UI SDK's Vue docs describe.
- **Layout can differ.** The elements have a wrapper tag around their parts (`<ui-select>`,
  `<ui-dialog>`); the native components render the parts alone. Placed straight into a
  grid, the native dialog trigger became the grid item and the element's did not.
- **You can skip the module.** With only the stylesheet and a plain element carrying the
  root's attributes, `data-uiset` and `data-skin`, the native button and switch were styled
  the same and no custom element was registered. You then have no `<uiset-*>` elements.

```ts
// The entry of a page that uses the stylesheet only
import { createApp } from "vue"
import "@uiset/web/uiset.css"
import CssOnly from "./CssOnly.vue"

createApp(CssOnly).mount("#app")
```

```vue
<div data-uiset :data-skin="skin">
  <Button data-variant="solid">Save</Button>
  <label>
    <Switch v-model="emails"><SwitchThumb /></Switch>
    Email me
  </label>
</div>
```

Both kinds can share a page: the comparison rendered them in one root. Other components
were not compared.

## Server rendering

What was tested is Vue's own server renderer (`renderToString`, then `createSSRApp`
hydrating in the browser, built with Vite's `--ssr` build). Nuxt was not tested.

- **The module imports on a server** (0.3.0 or later). It defines nothing there, so code
  that runs in both places can import it.
- **The server sends the tags and their text attributes.** Arrays, objects and functions
  are left out; Vue sets them as properties as it hydrates.
- **`v-model` doesn't compile for the server.** Vue's server compiler allows it on
  `<input>`, `<textarea>` and `<select>` only, so a server-rendered app binds the value and
  listens, as in [Two-way binding](#two-way-binding).

An element draws itself as soon as it's defined, and Vue expects to hydrate the HTML it
rendered. So mark the container Vue hydrates with `data-uiset-hydrating` in the server's
HTML, define the elements before Vue hydrates, and remove the attribute once it has. Under
it the elements are defined, so Vue finds their properties and sets your arrays and
functions on them, but they wait to draw until the attribute goes:

```html
<!-- index.html: the server's HTML goes inside -->
<div id="app" data-uiset-hydrating><!--app-html--></div>
```

```ts
// src/entry-client.ts
import "./elements" // everything that defines custom elements, @uiset/web included
import { createSSRApp } from "vue"
import App from "./App.vue"

createSSRApp(App).mount("#app")
document.getElementById("app")!.removeAttribute("data-uiset-hydrating")
```

The templates stay as they are: `:rows="rows"` with no `.prop`. Vue hydrates without a
mismatch, then the grid, the chart, the stepper and the patch bay draw with your data.
`<uiset-root>` doesn't wait, so the skin is there from the start, and until the module
runs a button inside `<ui-button>` looks like the browser's own.

Without the attribute, neither order works: defined before Vue hydrates, the app shell has
already laid out its children and Vue throws the page's HTML away; defined after, Vue
writes arrays as attributes (`rows="[object Object],…"`) and the grid stays empty. In Nuxt
the same shape should apply (the attribute on the app's root element, removed once the app
has mounted); that is untested.

## Agents

UI SDK's agent bridge reads the page's elements, whatever rendered them. Create it from the
Web Components entry, and an agent's steps fire the same events your template listens for:

```ts
import { createAgent } from "@ui-sdk/web/agent"

const agent = createAgent()
const result = ref("")

async function act() {
  const done = await agent.act({
    steps: [
      { ref: "Email me", action: "setChecked", args: [true] },
      { ref: "Orders", action: "selectRows", args: [["Grace Hopper"]] },
    ],
  })
  result.value = done.ok ? "ok" : String(done.error)
}
```

What each kit offers agents, approvals and the Agent Console are in
[Web Components](./web-components.md#agent-console) and
[Building with AI agents](./ai.md).

## What was tested

On 2026-11-19, the first screen above in a new app, with `@uiset/web` 0.4.0 and UI SDK
0.1.0-beta.10 from npm (`npm install @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web`), Vue 3.5.45, Vite 8.3.8 and
`vue-tsc` 3.3.14. It typechecks with default settings and with `strictTemplates` and the
declarations above, builds, and in Chrome its elements upgrade, take the base skin and
update Vue's state. The run through every code block on this page, next, was on beta.5.

On 2026-11-16, in a new Vite app from the `vue-ts` template: Vue 3.5.45, Vite 8.3.8,
`@vitejs/plugin-vue` 6.0.11, `vue-tsc` 3.3.14 and TypeScript 6.0.3, with `@uiset/web`
0.2.0 from a local build (0.2.0 never went to npm; 0.3.0 carries its changes), `@ui-sdk/web`, `@ui-sdk/core` and `@ui-sdk/vue`
0.1.0-beta.5, on Node 24.21 and npm 11.19. The app typechecks (default settings and
`strictTemplates`) and builds, also in a clean install with no `shiki`. Every code block on
this page ran in it, and the production build was driven in Chrome 157 with Playwright:
elements upgrading, properties arriving, events updating state, and skins read from
computed styles.

On 2026-11-17, against a later local build of 0.2.0 (Vue 3.5.45, Vite 7.3.8,
`@vitejs/plugin-vue` 6.0.11, `vue-tsc` 3.3.14): `v-model` on the eleven elements that
gained it (the search field had it already), driven in Chrome and WebKit (each element
shows the state it's given, a person's change reaches the state, and state set later
reaches the element); the typed `onCellEdit` block with `vue-tsc`; and the server rendering
recipe, rendered with `renderToString` and hydrated in Chrome and WebKit with no mismatch.


<!-- docs/svelte.md -->

# Svelte

UISet works in Svelte 5 through its Web Components build, `@uiset/web`: one module that
defines the `<uiset-*>` elements and one stylesheet with every skin. It's built on UI SDK,
whose own `<ui-*>` elements it dresses. This page covers what is specific to Svelte: setup,
passing data with runes, events, skins, UI SDK's Svelte components and server rendering.
Every element's attributes, properties and events are in
[Web Components](./web-components.md).

This page describes `@uiset/web` 0.3.0 or later.

## Install

```bash
npm install @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web
```

With npm this resolves `@ui-sdk/web` and `@ui-sdk/core` to `0.1.0-beta.10`, the exact
version UISet pins. pnpm takes UI SDK's `latest` tag, the same beta today, which moves on with
UI SDK's next one, so name the versions:

```bash
pnpm add @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web@0.1.0-beta.10 @ui-sdk/core@0.1.0-beta.10
```

`shiki` is optional: with it, code in chats is colored; without it the app still builds and
code blocks are plain.

Svelte needs no configuration for the tags. Vite's `svelte-ts` template works as it comes.

## A first screen

Import the UI SDK elements you use, then UISet's module and stylesheet, before the app
mounts. `uiset.css` already includes UI SDK's own styles.

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { mount } from "svelte"
import "@ui-sdk/web/button"
import "@ui-sdk/web/dialog"
import "@ui-sdk/web/select"
import "@ui-sdk/web/switch"
import "@uiset/web"
import "@uiset/web/uiset.css"
import "./app.css"
import App from "./App.svelte"

const app = mount(App, { target: document.getElementById("app")! })

export default app
```

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  const steps = [
    { value: "account", label: "Account" },
    { value: "details", label: "Details" },
    { value: "review", label: "Review" },
  ]
  let step = $state("details")
  let emails = $state(false)
</script>

<uiset-root skin="base">
  <ui-button><button>Save</button></ui-button>
  <ui-button><button data-variant="outline">Cancel</button></ui-button>

  <!-- svelte-ignore a11y_label_has_associated_control -->
  <label>
    <ui-switch oncheckedchange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: boolean }>) => (emails = e.detail.value)}>
      <ui-switch-thumb></ui-switch-thumb>
    </ui-switch>
    Email me
  </label>

  <uiset-stepper
    label="Setup progress"
    {steps}
    value={step}
    onvaluechange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: string }>) => (step = e.detail.value)}
  ></uiset-stepper>

  <uiset-stat label="Revenue" value="$48,200" change="12%" direction="up" period="vs last month"></uiset-stat>

  <p>Step: {step}. Emails: {emails ? "on" : "off"}.</p>
</uiset-root>
```

`<uiset-root>` holds the skin; everything inside takes it.

Svelte's accessibility checks don't know the elements. A `<label>` around `<ui-switch>`
warns that it has no control, though UI SDK names the switch from that label when it
upgrades; and the `<button>` inside `<ui-select-trigger>` warns that it has no text, though
`<ui-select-value>` fills it. The `svelte-ignore` comment above quiets the first, and
`a11y_consider_explicit_label` the second.

## Data in

Write arrays, objects and functions as ordinary attributes in braces. With the elements
defined before the app mounts (the imports in `main.ts` see to that), Svelte sets them as
properties, and text such as `label` as attributes.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import type { UISetDataGridEvents } from "@uiset/web"
  import { orders, type Order } from "./data"

  let rows = $state.raw<Order[]>(orders)
  const columns = [
    { id: "customer", header: "Customer", value: (o: Order) => o.customer, editable: true },
    { id: "plan", header: "Plan", value: (o: Order) => o.plan, options: ["Free", "Pro", "Team"] },
    { id: "seats", header: "Seats", type: "number", value: (o: Order) => o.seats, editable: true },
  ]
  const getRowId = (o: Order) => o.id

  let query = $state("")
  let selected = $state.raw<string[]>([])

  type CellEdit = UISetDataGridEvents<Order>["celledit"]

  function onCellEdit(event: CellEdit) {
    const { rowId, column, value } = event.detail
    if (column === "seats" && Number(value) < 1) return event.preventDefault()
    rows = rows.map((o) => (o.id === rowId ? { ...o, [column]: value } : o))
  }

  function addOrder() {
    rows = [...rows, { id: `o${rows.length + 1}`, customer: "New customer", plan: "Free", seats: 1 }]
  }
</script>

<uiset-search-field
  label="Search orders"
  placeholder="Search orders…"
  value={query}
  onvaluechange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: string }>) => (query = e.detail.value)}
></uiset-search-field>

<uiset-data-grid
  label="Orders"
  selectable
  editable
  height="16rem"
  {rows}
  {columns}
  {getRowId}
  {query}
  {selected}
  onselectedchange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: string[] }>) => (selected = e.detail.value)}
  oncelledit={onCellEdit}
></uiset-data-grid>
```

Functions are properties too. A chart takes its data and the functions that read it, and
`$derived` feeds a sparkline:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { months, type Month } from "./data"

  let data = $state.raw<Month[]>(months)
  const x = (d: Month) => d.month
  const series = [
    { key: "revenue", label: "Revenue", value: (d: Month) => d.revenue },
    { key: "costs", label: "Costs", value: (d: Month) => d.costs },
  ]
  const format = (n: number) => `$${n / 1000}k`
  let pinned = $state<string | null>(null)
  const revenue = $derived(data.map((d) => d.revenue))
</script>

<uiset-line-chart
  label="Revenue"
  description="By month"
  {data}
  {x}
  {series}
  {format}
  selected={pinned}
  onselect={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: string | null }>) => (pinned = e.detail.value)}
></uiset-line-chart>
<uiset-sparkline label="Revenue, five months" values={revenue}></uiset-sparkline>
```

Five things to know:

- **Replace arrays, don't change them in place.** An element redraws when its property is
  set again. `rows.push(…)` on deep `$state` changes your state and leaves the grid as it
  was; `rows = [...rows, row]` redraws it. `$state.raw` fits: the element gets your plain
  array, and only replacing it counts as a change.
- **Define the elements before Svelte renders them.** On a page that hydrated before the
  module loaded, arrays still arrived as properties and functions did not: the chart had no
  `x` and drew nothing.
- **A value set as a property leaves no attribute.** `<ui-select-item value="studio">` has
  no `value` attribute in the page, so don't select on it in CSS or tests.
- **An attribute that turns something on** (`selectable`, `editable`, `toolbar`, the
  root's `sound`) is written bare, as above, or given a boolean. `false` turns it off
  (0.3.0 or later):

```svelte
<uiset-data-grid toolbar={flags.toolbar}></uiset-data-grid>
```

- **A list can be text or an array** (0.3.0 or later). A sparkline's `values` and a stat's
  `trend` take either; an empty place in the text is a gap:

```svelte
<uiset-sparkline label="Trend" values="4,6,,8"></uiset-sparkline>
<uiset-sparkline label="Trend" values={[4, 6, null, 8]}></uiset-sparkline>
<uiset-stat label="Revenue" value="$48,200" trend="31,35,33,40,48"></uiset-stat>
```

## Events out

The elements report changes as DOM events, named in lowercase, with the new value in
`event.detail`. Listen with `on` and the event's name:

| Element                | Listener           | `event.detail`                                  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `<ui-switch>`          | `oncheckedchange`  | `value`: on or off                              |
| `<ui-select>`          | `onvaluechange`    | `value`: the chosen item's value                |
| `<uiset-stepper>`      | `onvaluechange`    | `value`: the step                               |
| `<uiset-search-field>` | `onvaluechange`    | `value`: the text                               |
| `<uiset-data-grid>`    | `onselectedchange` | `value`: the selected row ids                   |
| `<uiset-data-grid>`    | `oncelledit`       | `rowId`, `column`, `value`; `preventDefault()` refuses the edit |
| `<uiset-line-chart>`   | `onselect`         | `value`: the pinned position's key, or `null`   |
| `<uiset-patch-bay>`    | `onvaluechange`    | `value`: the cables, `[{ from, to }]`           |
| `<uiset-knob>`         | `onvaluechange`    | `value`: a number                               |

Setting a property fires no event, like a native input, so writing state back into an
element never loops.

## Two-way binding

`bind:value` doesn't compile on these elements: Svelte allows it on `<input>`,
`<textarea>` and `<select>` only. Pass the value and listen for the change:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  type Cable = { from: string; to: string }

  let jacks = $state.raw([
    { port: "lfo:out", name: "LFO out" },
    { port: "env:out", name: "Envelope out" },
    { port: "cutoff:in", name: "Cutoff in" },
    { port: "pitch:in", name: "Pitch in" },
  ])
  let cables = $state.raw<Cable[]>([{ from: "lfo:out", to: "cutoff:in" }])
  let level = $state(40)
</script>

<uiset-patch-bay
  aria-label="Patch bay"
  value={cables}
  onvaluechange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: Cable[] }>) => (cables = e.detail.value)}
>
  {#each jacks as jack (jack.port)}
    <uiset-patch-bay-jack value={jack.port}>
      <button aria-label={jack.name}></button>
    </uiset-patch-bay-jack>
  {/each}
</uiset-patch-bay>

<span id="level-label">Level</span>
<uiset-knob
  aria-labelledby="level-label"
  value={level}
  onvaluechange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: number }>) => (level = e.detail.value)}
>
  <uiset-knob-indicator></uiset-knob-indicator>
  <uiset-knob-value></uiset-knob-value>
</uiset-knob>
```

The same pair works for `checked` and `oncheckedchange` on `<ui-switch>`, `value` and
`onvaluechange` on `<ui-select>`, `selected` and `onselectedchange` on the grid, and
`selected` and `onselect` on a chart.

For a real `bind:`, wrap an element in a component with a `$bindable` prop:

```svelte
<!-- StepperField.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  type Step = { value: string; label: string; description?: string }

  let { value = $bindable(), steps, label }: { value: string; steps: Step[]; label?: string } = $props()
</script>

<uiset-stepper {label} {steps} {value} onvaluechange={(e: CustomEvent<{ value: string }>) => (value = e.detail.value)}
></uiset-stepper>
```

```svelte
<StepperField bind:value={wrapped} label="Wrapped" {steps} />
```

## Children

- **Elements that keep your children**: the root, `<ui-button>` around its button, a patch
  bay around its jacks. `{#each}` and `{#if}` work inside them; a jack added from state
  joins the bay.
- **Elements that draw themselves** (the grid, charts, the stepper, the search field, the
  stat): give them no children.
- **The app shell moves its children** into its sidebar, header and main area. They keep
  updating there, and `{#if}` works inside them and straight under the shell: a child that
  appears later is placed in the main area after the others, and leaves again (0.3.0 or
  later).

## The element from script

`bind:this` gives you the element, with the properties and methods
[Web Components](./web-components.md) lists. The package exports a type for each element:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { iconElement, type UISetDataGrid } from "@uiset/web"

  let grid = $state<UISetDataGrid>()
  let counted = $state(0)
  function count() {
    counted = grid?.rows.length ?? -1
  }

  function icon(node: HTMLElement) {
    node.append(iconElement("check"))
  }
</script>

<uiset-data-grid bind:this={grid} label="Deep rows" rows={deepRows} {columns} {getRowId}></uiset-data-grid>
<span id="icon" use:icon></span>
```

## TypeScript

- **The package ships its types** (0.3.0 or later): the functions it exports, a type for
  each element with options of its own (`UISetDataGrid`, `UISetStepper`, `UISetPatchBay`
  and the rest; charts and the grid take your row type, as in `UISetLineChart<Month>` and
  `UISetDataGrid<Order>`), and entries in
  `HTMLElementTagNameMap`, so `document.querySelector("uiset-data-grid")` is typed.
- **Markup needs nothing.** `svelte-check` accepts the tags as they are: an unknown tag
  takes any attribute.
- **Events are typed in script.** `grid.addEventListener("celledit", (e) => …)` knows
  `e.detail`. In markup, name a handler's parameter by the element's event map,
  exported with the elements: `UISetDataGridEvents<Order>["celledit"]`, as `onCellEdit`
  does, or `UISetKnobEvents["valuechange"]`.
- **To have a tag's attributes checked**, declare it in `svelte/elements`. The element's
  type gives its properties; attributes and events are yours to list, since the type
  describes the element and not what Svelte writes on it. Its events are then typed where
  you listen:

```ts
// src/uiset-elements.d.ts
import type { UISetStepper, UISetStepperEvents } from "@uiset/web"
import type { HTMLAttributes } from "svelte/elements"

// Types for the UISet elements this app uses. Undeclared tags stay unchecked.
declare module "svelte/elements" {
  interface SvelteHTMLElements {
    "uiset-stepper": HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement> & {
      label?: string
      value?: string
      linear?: boolean | "false"
      steps?: UISetStepper["steps"]
      onvaluechange?: (event: UISetStepperEvents["valuechange"]) => void
    }
  }
}
```

```svelte
<uiset-stepper label="Setup progress" {steps} value={step} onvaluechange={(e) => (step = e.detail.value)}
></uiset-stepper>
```

## Skins and themes

The root's attributes are ordinary attributes, and changing them restyles everything
inside at once. See [Theming](./theming.md) for the skins and their variables.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  let skin = $state("base")
  let theme = $state<"light" | "dark" | undefined>(undefined)
  let sound = $state(false)
</script>

<uiset-root {skin} {theme} {sound}>
```

| Attribute | Values                                                                        |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `skin`    | `"base"`, `"blueprint"`, `"studio"`, `"phosphor"` or `"ink"`                  |
| `theme`   | `"light"` or `"dark"`; `undefined` removes it and the page follows the system |
| `sound`   | `true` for interaction sounds, `false` for none (0.3.0 or later)              |

The themed skins have one scheme each (Studio is dark, Ink is light), so, as
[Theming](./theming.md#skins) says, `theme` is for the base skin.

### The key color

`<uiset-root>` has no key color attribute. Set what the React root sets: `data-key` and
three variables, the color's OKLCH lightness, chroma and hue.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  let key = $state({ l: 0.55, c: 0.2, h: 150 })
</script>

<uiset-root
  skin="base"
  data-key
  style:--uiset-key-l={key.l}
  style:--uiset-key-c={key.c}
  style:--uiset-key-h={key.h}
>
  <ui-button><button>Green key</button></ui-button>
</uiset-root>
```

### One skin inside another

The nearest root wins, so a root inside a root gives a panel its own skin or theme. It is
only as tall as what's in it (0.3.0 or later).

```svelte
<uiset-root {skin} {theme}>
  <uiset-root skin="blueprint">
    <ui-button><button>Blueprint</button></ui-button>
  </uiset-root>

  <uiset-root skin="base" theme="light">
    <ui-button><button>Always light</button></ui-button>
  </uiset-root>
</uiset-root>
```

### Fonts

The base skin uses your app's own font: the root and its controls inherit it (0.3.0 or
later). Each themed skin names its faces and falls back to system fonts. Load the ones you
use, for example Studio's from Google Fonts in `index.html`:

```html
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Saira+Semi+Condensed:wght@400;500;600&display=swap"
/>
```

The faces for each skin are listed in [Installation](./installation.md#fonts).

## UI SDK's Svelte components with UISet's look

UI SDK also ships native Svelte components, `@ui-sdk/svelte`. They work with UISet's
stylesheet: they render the same parts with the same `data-slot` and state attributes, and
`uiset.css` styles those attributes. Install the version UISet pins:

```bash
npm install @ui-sdk/svelte@0.1.0-beta.10
```

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { Button } from "@ui-sdk/svelte/button"
  import {
    Dialog,
    DialogBackdrop,
    DialogClose,
    DialogContent,
    DialogDescription,
    DialogTitle,
    DialogTrigger,
  } from "@ui-sdk/svelte/dialog"
  import {
    Select,
    SelectContent,
    SelectItem,
    SelectLabel,
    SelectTrigger,
    SelectValue,
  } from "@ui-sdk/svelte/select"
  import { Switch, SwitchThumb } from "@ui-sdk/svelte/switch"

  let emails = $state(false)
  let role = $state<string | null>(null)
</script>

<uiset-root skin="studio">
  <Button data-variant="solid">Save</Button>
  <Button data-variant="outline">Cancel</Button>
  <label>
    <Switch bind:checked={emails}><SwitchThumb /></Switch>
    Email me
  </label>
  <Select bind:value={role} placeholder="Select a role">
    <SelectLabel>Role</SelectLabel>
    <SelectTrigger><SelectValue /></SelectTrigger>
    <SelectContent>
      <SelectItem value="viewer">Viewer</SelectItem>
      <SelectItem value="editor">Editor</SelectItem>
    </SelectContent>
  </Select>
  <Dialog>
    <DialogTrigger>Share</DialogTrigger>
    <DialogBackdrop />
    <DialogContent>
      <DialogTitle>Share link</DialogTitle>
      <DialogDescription>Anyone with the link can view this.</DialogDescription>
      <DialogClose>Done</DialogClose>
    </DialogContent>
  </Dialog>
</uiset-root>
```

What was compared, in the base and Studio skins: the button (solid, outline and with
keyboard focus), the switch (off and on), the select (label, trigger, value, open list and
items) and the dialog (trigger, content, title, description, close and backdrop), each
beside the same control written with the custom elements.

- **The look is the same.** Every computed style on every part matched, apart from what a
  browser gives a tag before any stylesheet: the native switch is a `<button>`, with a
  button's text color and alignment, which a switch doesn't draw with. Screenshots of the
  buttons, the switch, the select's label and trigger, and the open dialog matched.
- **`bind:` works** on the native components, as UI SDK's Svelte docs describe.
- **The markup differs.** The elements have a wrapper tag around their parts
  (`<ui-select>`, `<ui-dialog>`); the native components render the parts alone, so there
  is no `[data-slot="select"]` element to style or select.
- **You can skip the module.** With only the stylesheet and a plain element carrying the
  root's attributes, `data-uiset` and `data-skin`, the native button and switch were styled
  the same and no custom element was registered. You then have no `<uiset-*>` elements.

```ts
// The entry of a page that uses the stylesheet only
import { mount } from "svelte"
import "@uiset/web/uiset.css"
import "./app.css"
import CssOnly from "./CssOnly.svelte"

export default mount(CssOnly, { target: document.getElementById("app")! })
```

```svelte
<div data-uiset data-skin={skin}>
  <Button data-variant="solid">Save</Button>
  <label>
    <Switch bind:checked={emails}><SwitchThumb /></Switch>
    Email me
  </label>
</div>
```

Both kinds can share a page: the comparison rendered them in one root. Other components
were not compared.

## Server rendering

What was tested is Svelte's own server renderer (`render` from `svelte/server`, then
`hydrate` in the browser, built with Vite's `--ssr` build). SvelteKit was not tested.

- **The module imports on a server** (0.3.0 or later). It defines nothing there, so code
  that runs in both places can import it.
- **The server writes every value into the HTML as text.** An array becomes
  `rows="[object Object],…"` and a function becomes its source, as in
  `getrowid="(o) => o.id"`. The elements don't read those; Svelte sets the real values as
  properties as it hydrates.

An element draws itself as soon as it's defined, and Svelte expects to hydrate the HTML it
rendered. So mark the container Svelte hydrates with `data-uiset-hydrating` in the
server's HTML, define the elements before Svelte hydrates, and remove the attribute once it
has. Under it the elements are defined, so Svelte sets your arrays and functions on them as
properties, but they wait to draw until the attribute goes:

```html
<!-- index.html: the server's HTML goes inside -->
<div id="app" data-uiset-hydrating><!--app-html--></div>
```

```ts
// src/entry-client.ts
import "./elements" // everything that defines custom elements, @uiset/web included
import { hydrate } from "svelte"
import App from "./App.svelte"

hydrate(App, { target: document.getElementById("app")! })
document.getElementById("app")!.removeAttribute("data-uiset-hydrating")
```

The markup stays as it is. Svelte hydrates without a warning, then the grid, the chart,
the stepper and the patch bay draw with your data. `<uiset-root>` doesn't wait, so the skin
is there from the start, and until the module runs a button inside `<ui-button>` looks like
the browser's own.

Without the attribute, elements defined before Svelte hydrates have already drawn
themselves: Svelte reports that it failed to hydrate and renders the page again in the
browser. In SvelteKit the same shape should apply (the attribute on the app's root
element, removed once it has hydrated); that is untested.

## Agents

UI SDK's agent bridge reads the page's elements, whatever rendered them. Create it from the
Web Components entry, and an agent's steps fire the same events your markup listens for:

```ts
import { createAgent } from "@ui-sdk/web/agent"

const agent = createAgent()

let result = $state("")

async function act() {
  const done = await agent.act({
    steps: [
      { ref: "Email me", action: "setChecked", args: [true] },
      { ref: "Orders", action: "selectRows", args: [["Grace Hopper"]] },
    ],
  })
  result = done.ok ? "ok" : String(done.error)
}
```

What each kit offers agents, approvals and the Agent Console are in
[Web Components](./web-components.md#agent-console) and
[Building with AI agents](./ai.md).

## What was tested

On 2026-11-19, the first screen above in a new app, with `@uiset/web` 0.4.0 and UI SDK
0.1.0-beta.10 from npm (`npm install @uiset/web @ui-sdk/web`), Svelte 5.58.0, Vite 8.3.8 and
`svelte-check` 4.7.8. It passes `svelte-check` with no errors or warnings, builds, and in
Chrome its elements upgrade, take the base skin and update Svelte's state. The run through
every code block on this page, next, was on beta.5.

On 2026-11-16, in a new Vite app from the `svelte-ts` template (plain Vite, not
SvelteKit): Svelte 5.57.3, Vite 8.3.8, `@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte` 7.3.1, `svelte-check`
4.7.8 and TypeScript 6.0.3, with `@uiset/web` 0.2.0 from a local build (0.2.0 never went to npm; 0.3.0 carries its changes),
`@ui-sdk/web`, `@ui-sdk/core` and `@ui-sdk/svelte` 0.1.0-beta.5, on Node 24.21 and npm
11.19. The app passes `svelte-check` and builds, also in a clean install with no `shiki`.
Every code block on this page ran in it, and the production build was driven in Chrome 157
with Playwright: elements upgrading, properties arriving, events updating state, and skins
read from computed styles.

On 2026-11-17, against a later local build of 0.2.0 (Svelte 5.57.3, Vite 8.3.8,
`svelte-check` 4.7.8): the typed `onCellEdit` block and the `svelte/elements` declaration
with `svelte-check`, and the server rendering recipe, rendered with `render` and hydrated in
Chrome and WebKit with no warning.


<!-- docs/templates.md -->

# Templates: design plan

Step 5 of the owner's plan. A template is a whole page built only from UISet items, so
a developer starts from a working screen instead of a blank one, and every piece of it
stays the same component they'd use by hand. Install one, render it, replace the
sample data with yours.

## The set (complete-set rule)

What a product team ships before anything domain-specific:

| Template      | Screens                                                                        | Built from                                                     |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auth`        | Sign in, sign up, forgot password, reset password, verify code, and a layout  | Field, Input, PasswordInput, OtpInput, Checkbox, Button, Card, Alert |
| `dashboard`   | KPI row with trends, filter row (date range, segment), charts, recent activity | AppShell, Stat, LineChart, BarChart, SegmentedBar, DataGrid, Select, SegmentedControl |
| `settings`    | Profile, account and security, notifications, billing with usage, team, danger zone | AppShell, Tabs, Field, Switch, Meter, DataGrid, Dialog, AlertDialog, Toast |
| `admin`       | A records list with create, edit in a drawer, bulk actions and confirmed delete | DataGrid, Drawer, Field, Select, AlertDialog, Toast, EmptyState |
| `inbox`       | Folders, a message list, a reading pane, compose                               | AppShell, Listbox, Badge, Dialog, Textarea, TokenInput, Toast  |
| `chat-app`    | The chat kit as a full page: chats, thread, composer                           | Chat kit                                                       |
| `pricing`     | A landing section: plans with a monthly/yearly switch, comparison, FAQ         | SegmentedControl, Card, Accordion, Badge                       |
| `project-board` | A project's issues as a board or a list: sprint progress, filters, details, new issue | AppShell, PageHeader, Meter, Board kit, DataGrid, SegmentedControl, Dialog, Toast |
| `calendar-app` | Day, week and month views, a small month to jump, calendars to show or hide, what's next | AppShell, Scheduler kit, Calendar, Checkbox, Tooltip, Toast |

The project board and the calendar came with the Board and Scheduler kits (step 6).

## Rules for every template

- **Only UISet items.** No new behavior lives in a template; if a page needs one, it
  becomes an item first.
- **Sample data in one place** at the top of the file, typed, so replacing it is one
  edit. Handlers are props (`onSignIn`, `onSave`, `onDelete`) with sample defaults.
- **Responsive** down to 360px, with the shell's drawer below 48rem.
- **Agent-operable:** every control has a specific name (no two "Save" buttons on one
  page), destructive actions carry `data-agent-confirm`, secrets carry
  `data-agent-secret`.
- **Forms** validate on submit with UI SDK's Field errors, keep what was typed, and
  focus the first problem. Auth fields carry the right `autocomplete` (`inputHints`).
- **Every skin and theme** passes axe; each template has a keyboard-only e2e path.
- Templates are client components whose data arrives as props, so a Server Component
  (or a loader) can fetch it and pass it in.

## Delivery

Each template is a registry block whose files install under `components/ui/templates/`,
importing UISet items relatively, like every other item. The site shows each one live
at `/templates`, in the chosen skin, with its install command.

## Use

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/dashboard
```

Each template installs to `components/ui/templates/<name>.tsx` with every item it uses.
Render it, then replace its sample data:

| Template    | Render                                     | Plug in                                                          |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auth`      | `<SignInForm onSignIn={…} />` and the other four forms | Each handler returns nothing on success or a message to show |
| `dashboard` | `<DashboardTemplate orders={…} now={new Date()} />` | Every figure, chart and row comes from `orders`; ranges end at `now` |
| `settings`  | `<SettingsTemplate onSave={(section, data) => …} onAction={…} />` | Each form's `FormData` by section; `onAction` for change plan, add seats, update card, change photo |
| `admin`     | `<AdminTemplate defaultCustomers={…} onSave={…} onDelete={…} />` | Reject to keep the drawer open with a message |
| `inbox`     | `<InboxTemplate defaultMessages={…} now={new Date()} onSend={…} onMove={…} />` | Sending and folder moves go to your mail API |
| `chat-app`  | `<ChatAppTemplate assistant={…} commands={…} mentions={…} />` | An async generator of `text`, `reasoning`, `tool` and `sources` events |
| `pricing`   | `<PricingTemplate plans={…} lede={…} />`   | Plans, comparison rows and questions are props; "save n%" comes from the plans |
| `project-board` | `<ProjectBoardTemplate defaultCards={…} defaultLanes={…} columns={…} people={…} labels={…} onMove={…} onSave={…} />` | Both views share the cards and lanes; the last column counts as done; `onCreate` and `onDelete` too |
| `calendar-app` | `<CalendarAppTemplate defaultEvents={…} calendars={…} today={…} now={new Date()} onSave={…} onDelete={…} />` | Each event names its calendar, and the calendar's chart slot is its color; times are minutes in `timeZone` |

- Mount `<Toaster />` (from `toast`) once in your app; templates call `toast()`.
- Inside a page that already has a `<main>`, pass `contentElement="div"`.
- **Cascade layers:** UISet's styles live in layers, so any unlayered CSS in your app
  wins over them. A global `a { color: … }` would recolor a button rendered as a link;
  scope such rules to plain links, like `a:not([data-slot])`.

### Connecting a model to `chat-app`

```tsx
async function* assistant({ text, history, signal }: AssistantInput) {
  const response = await fetch("/api/chat", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ text, history }),
    signal,
  })
  const reader = response.body!.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader()
  for (;;) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read()
    if (done) return
    yield { type: "text", delta: value } as const
  }
}
```

With the AI SDK's UI stream, map its parts the same way: text deltas to `text`, reasoning
to `reasoning`, tool calls and results to `tool` (same `id` updates the card), and source
parts to `sources`.

## Checked

Every template passes axe in Base (light and dark), Blueprint and Studio, fits a 375px
phone without sideways scrolling, and has a keyboard path in the e2e suite. Agents drive
them by the names people see: the dashboard's date range, the customers grid, the inbox
list, the issue board, the calendar.

- **Project board:** the board stays mounted while the list shows, so the card dialog
  moves cards through it from either view and column limits hold. Each move offers Undo
  for that card alone.
- **Calendar:** `EventDialog` has no calendar field, so a new event goes on the first
  calendar that's shown. While the sidebar shows, its New event is the page's one; the
  toolbar's takes over once the sidebar moves into the drawer, so no two buttons share a
  name.


<!-- docs/theming.md -->

# Theming

How UISet looks comes from a skin: CSS variables for color, type, edges, sound and motion.
Behavior (keys, focus, screen readers, agents) never changes with it.

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/uiset
```

## The root

```tsx
import { UISet } from "@/components/ui/uiset"

<UISet skin="base" keyColor={{ l: 0.55, c: 0.2, h: 268 }} theme="system" sound>
  <App />
</UISet>
```

| Prop       | Default    | What it does                                                                  |
| ---------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `skin`     | `"base"`   | `"base"`, `"blueprint"`, `"studio"`, `"phosphor"` or `"ink"`                  |
| `keyColor` | none       | `{ l, c, h }` in OKLCH: the base skin's accent (black and white without one)   |
| `theme`    | `"system"` | `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` (follows the device)                        |
| `sound`    | `false`    | Short synthesized sounds on interaction, voiced per skin                      |
| `haptics`  | `true`     | A tap on Android, and the system haptic on iOS 18 Safari, for switches and the like |

Every UISet item and every UI SDK component inside takes the skin, popups included: UI SDK
renders them in place, in the browser's top layer, so they inherit it. Web Components use `<uiset-root skin="ink" theme="light"
sound>` the same way.

## Skins

| Skin        | Look                                                                    | Scheme | Faces to load                   |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------- |
| `base`      | Your shadcn theme, one built from `keyColor`, or black and white        | both   | none (your app's)               |
| `blueprint` | A technical drawing: cyanotype paper, linework, hatching                | dark   | Barlow Semi Condensed           |
| `studio`    | A synth rack: gunmetal panels, rubber pads, amber lamps                 | dark   | Saira Semi Condensed            |
| `phosphor`  | A green-screen terminal: intensity, inverse video, faint scan lines     | dark   | Spline Sans Mono                |
| `ink`       | E-paper: ink on grey, dotted greys, a reading serif, no motion at all   | light  | Literata, Atkinson Hyperlegible |

Each skin falls back to system faces when its own aren't loaded; load them from Google
Fonts or self-host them for the intended look. The themed skins have one scheme, so
`theme` doesn't change them. The design notes for each are in `docs/studio.md`,
`docs/phosphor.md` and `docs/ink.md`.

Every skin is checked in every component and kit, in each scheme it has: text 4.5:1,
control edges and focus 3:1 (axe in the test suite), chart colors told apart with color
blindness (`tests/unit/chart-palette.test.ts`).

## The key color

The base skin builds its accent from one OKLCH color: solid buttons, checked controls,
the selected day, focus rings. Text on it picks black or white by lightness, dark mode
lifts the ring toward white so it stays visible, and the grays lean slightly toward its hue.

With no `keyColor` and no shadcn theme on the page, the base skin is black and white: a
near-black accent (near-white in dark mode) on neutral grays, the look of shadcn/ui's
default theme and of uiset.dev.

### A whole theme from one color

The [theme generator](https://uiset.dev/themes/generator) goes further than a key
color. From one color, a neutral tint, a radius, a density and a text size, it builds every
token for light and dark: surfaces, text, edges, focus, the four status tones and eight
chart colors. It checks 32 pairs in each scheme (text 4.5:1, controls and focus 3:1, chart
colors 3:1 and apart under color blindness), moves any derived color that fails to the
nearest lightness that passes, and offers a one-click fix when the key itself fails.

It exports the result three ways: a UISet skin file (use it with `skin="custom"`, or the
name you give it), shadcn/ui variables for `:root` and `.dark`, and W3C design tokens. The
address keeps every setting, so a link reopens the same theme.

### With a shadcn/ui theme

With no `keyColor`, the base skin adopts the shadcn theme already on the page:
`--background`, `--foreground`, `--muted`, `--muted-foreground`, `--border`, `--input`,
`--primary` and `--radius`, with `--primary-foreground` for text on the accent. UISet
components then match the rest of your app, solid buttons hover the way shadcn/ui's do,
and your theme switcher keeps working.

## Dark mode

`theme="system"` follows the device; `"light"` and `"dark"` pin it for the subtree. The
base skin's colors use `light-dark()`, so a light section inside a dark page is just
another `<UISet theme="light">`.

## Nesting

Skins only set variables, so the nearest root wins. A Blueprint panel inside a Base app:

```tsx
<UISet skin="base">
  <Settings />
  <UISet skin="blueprint">
    <Schematic />
  </UISet>
</UISet>
```

## Your own parts

Style your own markup with the variables, and it follows every skin:

| Variable                                   | What it is                                      |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `--ui-background`, `--ui-foreground`       | The surface and its text                        |
| `--ui-muted`, `--ui-muted-foreground`      | Quiet surfaces, and secondary text (4.5:1)      |
| `--ui-border`, `--ui-input`                | Hairlines, and control edges (3:1)              |
| `--ui-primary`, `--ui-primary-foreground`  | The accent and text on it                       |
| `--ui-ring-border`                         | Focus rings                                     |
| `--ui-radius`, `--ui-font-sans`, `--ui-font-mono` | Corners and faces                         |
| `--tone-info`, `--tone-success`, `--tone-warning`, `--tone-danger` | Status colors, readable as text |
| `--chart-1` … `--chart-8`, `--chart-seq-1` … `--chart-seq-7` | Data colors, in a fixed order     |

## Writing a skin

A skin is a stylesheet in the `uiset.skin` layer that sets variables on its own selector:

```css
@layer ui-sdk, uiset.tokens, uiset.base, uiset.skin;

@layer uiset.skin {
  [data-uiset][data-skin="harbor"] {
    color-scheme: light;
    --ui-background: oklch(0.97 0.01 220);
    --ui-foreground: oklch(0.25 0.03 230);
    --ui-primary: oklch(0.45 0.12 230);
    --ui-primary-foreground: white;
    /* …and the rest of the table above */
  }
}
```

Then `<UISet skin="harbor">`. Keep the contrast rules (text 4.5:1, edges and focus 3:1),
and check it the way UISet's skins are checked: add it to the skin loops in
`tests/e2e/components.spec.ts` and run axe. Decoration a variable can't express (a
texture, a bevel) may use selectors under the same `[data-uiset][data-skin]`, so nested
skins never inherit it.

## Sound and haptics

`sound` turns on short sounds for presses, toggles, selection and errors, made with Web
Audio (no files). Each skin picks a voice (`--uiset-sound`: `soft`, `mechanical`, `beep`
or `paper`); `--uiset-sound-volume` sets the level. Sounds follow UI SDK's own events, so
they play for agents' changes too. Haptics are on by default where the device has them.

## Motion and system settings

UISet's motion stops under `prefers-reduced-motion`; Ink has none at all. In Windows'
forced colors, state that relied on fills becomes borders, and Phosphor drops its bloom
and scan lines.


<!-- docs/migrate-from-shadcn.md -->

# Coming from shadcn/ui

UISet installs with the same CLI into the same folder, and its base skin adopts your
shadcn theme. What changes is underneath: components are UI SDK's, so keyboard, focus,
screen reader and agent behavior come built in, and the API follows UI SDK's.

## Moving an app over

If a coding agent is doing the move, give it the [Agent migration recipe](./agent-migration.md):
the same steps, written for an agent, with a check after each one.

1. **Commit first.** UISet items have the same file names as shadcn's
