   (`components/ui/button.tsx`), and the CLI asks before it overwrites one.
2. **Add the root** and wrap the app. Your theme variables are picked up as they are:

   ```bash
   npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/uiset
   ```

   ```tsx
   <UISet skin="base">
     <App />
   </UISet>
   ```

   Tailwind CSS 4 needs no setup; for server rendering there's one optional line
   ([With Tailwind CSS](./installation.md#with-tailwind-css)).

3. **Replace components one at a time.** Move the shadcn files that import shadcn's button
   (dialog, alert-dialog, sheet, calendar, pagination) before the button itself: UISet's
   button has no `buttonVariants` and none of shadcn's sizes, so replacing it first breaks
   them. Leaves like badge, input and checkbox can go at any time. With that order the app
   keeps building between steps.
4. **Run your tests.** Selectors by role and name keep working; selectors on Radix's
   `data-state` need the UI SDK attributes below.

## What maps to what

| shadcn/ui            | UISet item        | Notes                                                                 |
| -------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Button               | `button`          | `variant`: `solid` (default), `outline`, `ghost`; no `size` and no `buttonVariants` |
| Input, Label, Form   | `field`           | `Field`, `FieldLabel`, `Input`, `FieldDescription`, `FieldError`; native forms, no form library needed |
| Select               | `select`          | `SelectTrigger` shows the chosen value by itself; `SelectLabel` names it; `placeholder` goes on `Select`; `onValueChange` passes `string \| null` |
| DropdownMenu         | `menu`            | `Menu`, `MenuTrigger`, `MenuContent`, `MenuItem`; handle `onAction` on the menu |
| Dialog               | `dialog`          | `Dialog`, `DialogTrigger`, `DialogContent`, `DialogTitle`, `DialogClose`; no Header or Footer parts, use your own markup; `DialogBackdrop` dims the page |
| AlertDialog          | `alert-dialog`    | `AlertDialogClose` for both buttons (`value="confirm"` on the confirming one), `AlertDialogBackdrop`; no Header, Footer, Action or Cancel |
| Sheet                | `drawer`          | `Drawer`, with snap points and a handle; `side` goes on `Drawer`       |
| Popover, Tooltip, HoverCard | `popover`, `tooltip`, `hover-card` | Same idea, UI SDK's parts            |
| Tabs                 | `tabs`            | `TabsTab` for TabsTrigger, `TabsPanel` for TabsContent                |
| Accordion            | `accordion`       | `AccordionItem`, `AccordionTrigger`, `AccordionPanel` for AccordionContent |
| Command              | `command`         | `CommandInput`, `CommandList`, `CommandItem`, `CommandEmpty`          |
| Toast (Sonner)       | `toast`           | `toast("Saved", { description })`, with a `ToastRegion` in the app    |
| Checkbox, Switch, Slider, RadioGroup | `checkbox`, `switch`, `slider`, `radio` | Same use; Slider takes a number or an array |
| Calendar, DatePicker | `calendar`, `date-picker` | Values are ISO date strings (`value`, `onValueChange`); plus `date-input` and `time-input` for typed dates |
| Table, DataTable     | `data-grid`       | Sorting, filters, grouping, pinning, editing and virtual rows built in |
| Card, Badge, Alert, Skeleton, Breadcrumb | `card`, `badge`, `alert`, `skeleton`, `breadcrumbs` | See [App frame and data display](./app-shell.md) |
| Sidebar              | `app-shell`       | A sidebar that collapses to icons and becomes a drawer on phones      |
| Chart (Recharts)     | `line-chart`, `bar-chart`, … | No chart library: keyboard-explorable, with a table view    |

Things shadcn/ui doesn't have: the [chat kit](./chat.md), a
[rich text editor](./rich-text.md), [board](./board.md), [scheduler](./scheduler.md),
[canvas](./canvas.md), [IDE](./ide.md), [terminal](./terminal.md), the
[Agent Console](./agent-console.md) and [whole-page templates](./templates.md).

## API differences

- **`asChild` becomes `render`.** `<Button asChild><a href="/">Home</a></Button>` is
  `<Button render={<a href="/" />}>Home</Button>`.
- **State attributes.** Radix's `data-state="open"` and `data-state="checked"` are
  `data-open` and `data-checked` (also `data-pressed`, `data-highlighted`,
  `data-disabled`). Every part has a `data-slot`, like `data-slot="dialog-content"`.
- **Change handlers** are `onValueChange`, `onOpenChange`, `onCheckedChange` and
  `onPressedChange`, with a second `details` argument that says why it changed (a click,
  a key, an agent) and can cancel it.
- **Styling.** UISet ships plain CSS in cascade layers, not Tailwind classes. Tailwind
  keeps working beside it: a class on any part wins over UISet's styles
  ([With Tailwind CSS](./installation.md#with-tailwind-css)).
- **Names for agents.** UI SDK's agent bridge finds controls by their accessible names.
  A control with a visible label is already named; an icon button needs `aria-label`.

## Theme

Nothing to change: the base skin reads `--background`, `--foreground`, `--muted`,
`--muted-foreground`, `--border`, `--input`, `--primary`, `--primary-foreground` and
`--radius`. Without a shadcn theme it's black and white; to set the accent, pass `keyColor`, or try one in the
[theme generator](https://uiset.dev/themes/generator), which also exports shadcn/ui variables. See [Theming](./theming.md).


<!-- docs/agent-migration.md -->

# Agent migration recipe

This page is written for a coding agent. It moves an app built with shadcn/ui (on Radix or
Base UI) to UISet, one component at a time, with a check after every step. The app builds at
every commit, and the people using it see the same screens. The person's version, with the
reasoning, is [Coming from shadcn/ui](./migrate-from-shadcn.md).

Give your agent this page:

```text
Move this app from shadcn/ui to UISet. Follow https://uiset.dev/docs/agent-migration.md
step by step. Run each step's check before starting the next, commit after each component,
and stop and tell me if a check fails twice.
```

An agent with the UISet skill (`npx skills add superzero11/uiset`) or Context7
(`/superzero11/uiset`) can look up every item's docs on its own.

The recipe was run end to end on a Vite app with 17 shadcn components (shadcn 4.23, Tailwind
4, React 19): about 20 commits, the build passing after each, and an agent-readiness score of
100 at the end.

## Before you start

The person does these:

- **React 19.** UI SDK needs it. Upgrade first if the app is on 18.
- **A clean branch.** Commit or stash everything, then branch.
- **Tests, if there are any.** The recipe leans on typecheck and build, and every test the app
  has makes a step safer.

## Rules for the agent

- **One component per step, one commit per step.** If a step breaks something you can't fix,
  reset to the last commit and report.
- **Don't change behavior or layout beyond the swap.** Same labels, same handlers, same data.
  Note anything that has to change in `MIGRATION.md` instead of improvising.
- **Behavior comes from UI SDK.** Never hand-write keyboard handling, focus traps or ARIA that
  a UI SDK component covers. Each component's API is in
  `node_modules/@ui-sdk/react/docs/components/<name>.md` once the root is installed.
- **Never let the CLI ask.** Without a terminal, `shadcn add` meets an existing file with
  "The file button.tsx already exists. Would you like to overwrite?", writes nothing, and
  still exits 0. Run `npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/<item> --dry-run` to see what it would
  overwrite, then add with `--overwrite` when replacing a shadcn file. `-y` doesn't skip that
  prompt.
- **Keep your own CSS out of `components/ui/uiset/`.** Every item depends on the root, so
  `--overwrite` rewrites the root's stylesheets too.

## Step 1: Take stock

Find the components folder (`aliases.ui` in `components.json`, usually
`src/components/ui` or `components/ui`), then list what's there, what uses it, and which
shadcn files import each other:

```bash
ls src/components/ui
grep -rhoE "from ['\"]@/components/ui/[a-z-]+['\"]" src | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep -lE "components/ui/button['\"]|from ['\"]\./button['\"]" src/components/ui/*.tsx
grep -oE '"(radix-ui|@radix-ui/[a-z-]+|@base-ui[a-z/-]*|cmdk|vaul|sonner|react-day-picker|date-fns|input-otp|embla-carousel-react|recharts|react-resizable-panels|class-variance-authority|tw-animate-css)"' package.json
```

Write `MIGRATION.md` with one row per file in the components folder: the shadcn file, how
many files import it, the UISet item from the table below, whether it's replaced in place or
added beside, and a status column. Mark the files the third command found: they import
shadcn's button.

**Check:** every file in the components folder has a row, and every import the second command
found points at a row.

## Step 2: Record the baseline

Run the app's typecheck, tests and build, and write the results in `MIGRATION.md`. Failures
that exist now aren't yours to fix; failures that appear later are.

**Check:** the baseline is in `MIGRATION.md`.

## Step 3: Add the root

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/uiset
```

Wrap the app's root (the layout in Next.js, `main.tsx` in Vite) once:

```tsx
import { UISet } from "@/components/ui/uiset"

export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <UISet skin="base">{children}</UISet>
}
```

The base skin reads the app's shadcn variables (`--background`, `--foreground`, `--primary`,
`--border`, `--radius` and the rest), so the theme carries over.

**Tailwind CSS 4 needs nothing here.** UISet puts its layer between Tailwind's reset and its
utilities, so the controls keep their look and the app's utility classes still win. If an
older copy of the root is installed (no `components/ui/uiset/layers.ts`), add it again with
`--overwrite`. In a server-rendered app (Next.js), also put
`@layer theme, base, uiset, components, utilities;` at the top of the global stylesheet, so the
first paint has that order too ([With Tailwind CSS](./installation.md#with-tailwind-css)).

Then pin UI SDK to the exact version the root installed, since npm saves it with a `^` and a
beta can change between versions:

```bash
npm install --save-exact @ui-sdk/core@<version> @ui-sdk/react@<version>
```

**Check:** typecheck and build pass, the pages render as before, and a `<button>` from UI SDK
on any page still has its padding and border.

## Step 4: Replace components, one at a time

**Order.** UISet's button doesn't export `buttonVariants`, and it has none of shadcn's sizes or
variant names, so replacing `button.tsx` first breaks every shadcn file that imports it (in the
test app: dialog, alert-dialog, sheet, calendar and pagination, 28 type errors). Move the files
Step 1 marked first, then the button. Leaves like badge, input, label, checkbox and switch can
go at any time. Do the sidebar, a data table, charts and forms last, each as its own step.

If one of the marked files has to wait, keep a copy of shadcn's button for it
(`git show HEAD:src/components/ui/button.tsx > src/components/ui/button-shadcn.tsx`), point
that file's import at the copy, and delete the copy when the last such file has moved.

For each component:

1. **Install it.** Same file name as shadcn's: `npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/<item>
   --overwrite`. Different name (the "added beside" rows below): `npx shadcn@latest add
   @uiset/<item>`, which leaves the old file in place.
2. **Typecheck.** Every error is a call site to update. Fix each with the notes below and the
   component's docs in `node_modules/@ui-sdk/react/docs/components/`. A prop that compiles
   isn't proof: shadcn's calendar `mode` and `selected` typecheck and do nothing.
3. **Move the imports** of an "added beside" item to the new file, then delete the old file.
4. **Update tests** that select by Radix's `data-state` (see "Everywhere" below).
5. **Check:** typecheck, tests and build pass, and `grep -r "components/ui/<old-name>" src`
   finds nothing for a deleted file. Mark the row done in `MIGRATION.md` and commit.

### What maps to what

These shadcn files have a UISet item of the same name, which replaces them in place:
`accordion`, `alert`, `alert-dialog`, `avatar`, `badge`, `button`, `calendar`, `card`,
`carousel`, `checkbox`, `collapsible`, `combobox`, `command`, `dialog`, `drawer`, `field`,
`hover-card`, `input`, `kbd`, `label`, `menubar`, `navigation-menu`, `pagination`, `popover`,
`progress`, `resizable`, `scroll-area`, `select`, `separator`, `skeleton`, `slider`,
`spinner`, `switch`, `table`, `tabs`, `textarea`, `toggle` and `tooltip`.

The rest have another name, or stay:

| shadcn/ui file | UISet item | Lands |
|---|---|---|
| `breadcrumb` | `breadcrumbs` | added beside |
| `dropdown-menu`, `context-menu` | `menu` | added beside |
| `input-otp` | `otp-input` | added beside |
| `radio-group` | `radio` | added beside |
| `sheet` | `drawer` | added beside |
| `sonner` | `toast` | added beside |
| `toggle-group` | `toggle` (`ToggleGroup`) | added beside |
| `input-group` | `input` (`InputGroup`) | added beside |
| `empty` | `empty-state` | added beside |
| `item` | `item-list` | added beside |
| `sidebar` | `app-shell` | added beside, as its own step at the end |
| a data table on TanStack Table | `data-grid` | added beside, as its own step |
| `chart` (Recharts) | `line-chart`, `bar-chart`, `scatter-chart`, `heatmap`, `segmented-bar` | added beside, as its own step |
| `form` (React Hook Form) | none: keep it | stays; connect each UISet control through a `Controller` |
| `aspect-ratio`, `typography`, `button-group` | none: keep them | stay |

### Component by component

What the test app needed, beyond renaming imports:

- **button.** Variants are `solid` (the default), `outline` and `ghost`: `default` becomes
  `solid`, `secondary` becomes `outline`, `link` becomes `ghost` rendering an `<a>`, and
  `destructive` becomes `solid` with your own class plus `data-agent-confirm` saying what it
  does. There's no `size`: drop it, and keep an `aria-label` on icon-only buttons. `asChild`
  becomes `render`: `<Button render={<a href="/docs" />}>Docs</Button>`.
- **Triggers and close buttons** of dialogs, menus and popovers are buttons themselves. Instead
  of wrapping a `Button` with `asChild`, put the label inside the trigger and give it
  `data-variant="solid"`, `"outline"` or `"ghost"` for a button's look.
- **dialog.** No `DialogHeader` or `DialogFooter`: use your own `<div>`s. Add `<DialogBackdrop />`
  for the dimmed page, and a `DialogClose` where shadcn drew its corner ×.
- **alert-dialog.** No `AlertDialogHeader`, `Footer`, `Action` or `Cancel`. Both buttons are
  `AlertDialogClose`; the confirming one takes `value="confirm"`. Add `<AlertDialogBackdrop />`.
- **dropdown-menu → menu.** `Menu`, `MenuTrigger`, `MenuContent`, `MenuItem`. Give each item a
  `value` and handle choices once with `onAction={(value) => …}` on `Menu`, instead of
  `onSelect` on each item. `variant="destructive"` on an item becomes `destructive`; a label is
  `MenuGroupLabel` inside a `MenuGroup`. A context menu is `Menu` with `MenuContextTrigger`.
- **select.** `onValueChange` passes `string | null`, so `setState` for a string needs
  `(v) => setValue(v ?? "")`. `placeholder` moves from `SelectValue` to `Select`, and
  `<SelectLabel>` inside the `Select` names it, in place of a separate `Label`.
- **tabs.** `TabsTrigger` is `TabsTab` and `TabsContent` is `TabsPanel`. Name the tabs
  (`<Tabs aria-label="Settings sections">`): an agent needs it.
- **accordion.** `AccordionContent` is `AccordionPanel`.
- **sonner → toast.** UISet's toast exports `toast` and `Toaster`, and
  `toast("Saved", { description })` reads the same. Only the imports change.
- **calendar.** Dates are ISO strings: `value="2026-11-17"` and `onValueChange`, in place of
  `mode`, `selected` and `onSelect` with `Date` objects.
- **pagination.** A different model: the parts become one
  `<Pagination aria-label="Results pages" pageCount={…} getHref={(page) => …} />`.
- **sheet → drawer.** `Sheet`, `SheetTrigger` and `SheetContent` become `Drawer`,
  `DrawerTrigger` and `DrawerContent`. `side` moves from the content to `Drawer`, and
  `<DrawerBackdrop />` dims the page.
- **badge.** `variant` becomes `tone`: `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning` or `danger`.
- **tooltip.** There's no `TooltipProvider`; remove it.
- **card.** Unchanged, except there's no `CardAction`.
- **checkbox, switch, input, label, field.** Drop-in.

### Everywhere

- **Change handlers** are `onValueChange`, `onOpenChange`, `onCheckedChange` and
  `onPressedChange`, with a second `details` argument that says why the value changed.
- **State attributes.** Radix's `data-state="open"` and `data-state="checked"` are
  `data-open` and `data-checked` (also `data-pressed`, `data-highlighted`, `data-disabled`),
  and every part has a `data-slot`.
- **Styling.** Tailwind classes on any part win over UISet's styles, so the app's own classes
  keep working.

## Step 5: Remove what nothing uses

When the last component that used a package is gone, uninstall it. shadcn's Radix style
depends on the `radix-ui` package (older apps on `@radix-ui/*`), plus `class-variance-authority`,
`tw-animate-css`, `sonner`, `react-day-picker` and `date-fns`:

```bash
grep -rl "from \"sonner\"" src || npm uninstall sonner
```

Do the same for each package Step 1 found, and delete `components/ui` files that nothing
imports. Keep `cn` in `lib/utils.ts` while the app's own code uses it, and remove the
`tw-animate-css` import from the stylesheet with its package.

**Check:** typecheck, tests and build pass.

## Step 6: Check that an agent can use it

An agent operates the app through UI SDK's agent bridge, so create one once, in its own module
imported by the app's entry (`main.tsx` in Vite, a client component in Next.js):

```ts
// src/agent.ts
import { createAgent, registerTools } from "@ui-sdk/react/agent"

const agent = createAgent()

// Ask a person before an agent presses anything.
const unregister = registerTools(agent, {
  allow: (step) => step.action !== "press" || confirm(`Press ${step.args[0]}?`),
})

// Vite only: drop the old tools when the module reloads.
if (import.meta.hot) import.meta.hot.dispose(unregister)

export { agent }
```

Then run the readiness check against the running app and its main pages:

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/agent-check
npx tsx src/components/ui/agent-check/cli.ts http://localhost:5173 /settings /billing
```

It uses the bridge when it finds one and scores each page. Add `--channel chrome` to use the
installed Chrome instead of downloading Playwright's Chromium. In the test app it found an unnamed
set of tabs, three names that each found two controls ("Save" in "Save profile", "Delete" in
"Delete account", "Email" in "Email notifications") and a Delete with no
`data-agent-confirm`. Fix each (a name, a more specific label, a confirmation), then add
`expectAgentReady` to the app's tests so it stays that way. See
[Agent readiness check](./agent-check.md).

**Check:** every page scores 100, or each remaining problem is listed in `MIGRATION.md` with
the reason it stays.

## Step 7: Report

Finish `MIGRATION.md` with:

- what moved, and the commits;
- what stayed and why (`form`, charts, anything UISet doesn't have);
- the agent-readiness score of each page;
- checks that fail, with the error.

Then hand it back to the person to review the branch.


<!-- docs/roadmap.md -->

# Roadmap

Updated 2026-11-19. What we're building, what comes next, and what we won't do. What
shipped is in the [changelog](https://github.com/superzero11/uiset/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md),
and the decisions behind it in
[HISTORY.md](https://github.com/superzero11/uiset/blob/main/HISTORY.md). Sizes: S small,
M medium, L large.

## How we order it

First, what UI SDK's own showcase of styled screens does and UISet doesn't yet: UISet should
already be past anything styled on UI SDK. Then what developers ask for most, by the votes on
shadcn/ui and UI SDK threads, then what nobody ships. Each piece has to beat a plainly styled
version: a kit around it, agents, five skins, sound and motion, and tests in all of them.

## Now

**Sortable lists and trees.** The sortable list and tree are in: drag or pick up with Space,
move a selection together, and nest rows by moving them sideways. Next, the IDE's file tree
lets a file be dragged into a folder. M

## Next, in order

1. **Motion, per skin.** Each skin moves its own way, as it already sounds its own way:
   openings, moves and state changes, drawn from UI SDK's state, reduced motion respected. M–L
2. **The inputs asked for most.** A tag input that creates and edits its chips, a phone
   number field with a country picker, and input masks for cards, IBANs and currency. M
3. **Data grid: filters and saved views.** A filter bar with typed operators, saved views,
   and agents setting a filter by name. M
4. **Emoji picker, draggable tabs and a media player.** Reactions in chat, IDE tabs that
   reorder, and a player whose scrubber snaps to chapters, beside Studio. M each
5. **Locale packs.** Every component's and kit's built-in words translated, with
   right-to-left tested packs for the main languages. UI SDK ships none. M
6. **Theme import and exports.** Bring in a tweakcn or shadcn/ui preset, with contrast
   repair; export to Tailwind `@theme`, Figma variables and DESIGN.md. S
7. **Data grid: remote rows, tree rows and detail rows.** Server sort, filter and cursor
   paging. M–L
8. **App shell variants.** Menus that fly out when the sidebar is collapsed, drill-down, a
   double sidebar, a top bar. M
9. **More templates.** Checkout, travel booking, profile, helpdesk tickets, a file manager
   and an invoice. S each
10. **Print skin.** Swiss and letterpress type, from a written design plan first. M
11. **SaaS console screens.** Team and roles, API keys and webhooks, an audit log, usage, CSV
    import. M

Between these, small ones: an agent migration recipe (UI SDK has none yet), dialogs and
popovers that open in place (UI SDK's `inline`), tree select, matches marked in combobox
results, an autocomplete that loads from a server, swiping a toast away, a context menu on
any area, an Angular guide, and focus that moves in the same task in the 24 places the lint
still lists.

## Then: motion and developer tools

- **Animated components, kits and templates**, built on the motion above: the Library's
  Animate column, with Illustrations (animated scenes for landing pages) and Motion (text,
  numbers, transitions), and kits and templates whose movement shows what changed. L
- **Developer tools:** Agent view as a browser extension for any UI SDK app; upgrade help,
  a per-item diff when UI SDK moves so your edits survive; a starter app with the templates
  as routed pages. M each

## Later

A map kit, a seat map, a Gantt chart, dragging onto dates and cards, a swipe deck and a
radial menu for the mobile kit, a window manager and resizable panels, sticky notes on the
canvas, a dashboard grid, a document viewer, voice in chat, the Cockpit and Paper skins, a
Solid guide, more templates (onboarding, an agent-wired settings console, a docs site), and
generative UI adapters.

## Following UI SDK

UI SDK is in public beta. UISet pins its exact version and moves with each release once the
tests for what the release changes pass. UISet is on 0.1.0-beta.10. Problems we find in UI SDK
go upstream with a test that shows them. Open now:
[#780](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/780) (a wheel in a drawer in WebKit),
[#887](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/887) (web scroll areas named from their root)
and [#888](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/888) (`createStickToBottom` with its rows in
a wrapper). Fixed for
the beta after beta.10: [#848](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/848) (a `run` action's
argument read as an item), [#856](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/856) (Pagination's
dev check) and [#857](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/857) (web tabs named by their
list).

## Waiting on others

- registry.directory is reviewing UISet's entry.
- [bytefer/awesome-shadcn-ui#61](https://github.com/bytefer/awesome-shadcn-ui/pull/61), quiet
  since 2026-11-16. birobirobiro/awesome-shadcn-ui listed UISet on 2026-11-18.

## Shipped so far

The root and five skins with sound and haptics; all 55 UI SDK components styled, plus app
frame, data display and form parts, and the small ones from UI SDK's showcase (scroll edge
fades, radio cards, rings, a textarea's count, password rules, a confirm button); twelve
kits (chat, rich text, data grid, charts, board, scheduler, canvas, IDE, mobile, terminal,
Studio, Agent Console); ten page templates; Web Components for every kit and template; a
schema form agents fill by field name; [agent-check](./agent-check.md), which scores whether
agents can use a page; and the theme generator.

## What we won't do

- Copy the look of a real product or brand. Every skin is an original design.
- Put a second UI library underneath. Behavior always comes from UI SDK.
- Use "Vercel" in a product name. UISet is a community project, not affiliated with Vercel.

## Asking for things

[Open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/superzero11/uiset/issues) with what you're
building and what's missing. Kits and templates that many people need come first.


<!-- docs/blueprint.md -->

# Blueprint

A technical drawing: cyanotype paper, white linework, hatching for filled states,
dimension lines for slider tracks, and lettering for labels. It was the first themed skin,
built to prove that a skin can change everything about how UI SDK's components look while
changing nothing about how they behave.

```tsx
<UISet skin="blueprint">…</UISet>
```

## Tokens

| Name   | Value                         | Role                                                   |
| ------ | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Paper  | `oklch(0.36 0.11 254)`        | The page: a deep cyanotype blue                        |
| Line   | `oklch(0.96 0.02 230)`        | Text, borders, fills: drawn in white                   |
| Faint  | Line at 16%                   | Hover fills and the fine grid                          |
| Grid   | Line at 7%                    | The 8px and 64px drawing grid on the paper             |
| Ring   | `oklch(0.9 0.13 200)`         | Focus: a cyan line, distinct from the white drawing    |

**Type.** Barlow Semi Condensed; labels and buttons in spaced capitals, like drafting
lettering.

**Drawing language.**

- Text boxes are a line to write on, not a box.
- Checked and filled states are hatched, not filled solid: a switch's track, a slider's
  range.
- Slider tracks are dimension lines with end ticks; the thumb is a diamond.
- Popups are a sheet laid on the drawing, with an offset shadow line.
- What isn't reached yet (an empty star, an upcoming step) is drawn faint.

**Scheme.** Dark only: `theme` doesn't change it.

**Contrast.** White linework on the paper clears 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for every control
edge; the chart colors are a set chosen for the blue paper and checked for color blindness
(neighbors CVD ΔE ≥ 14.6).


<!-- docs/studio.md -->

# Studio: design plan

**Subject.** A rack of synthesizer modules on a studio desk: painted metal faceplates,
rubber knob caps, silk-screened legends, amber indicator lamps and patch cables.
**Audience.** Developers building music, audio and creative tools, and anyone who wants
an interface that feels like hardware. **Job.** The demo that makes the skin system
obvious: the same UI SDK components, turned into instruments you can hear.

Not SPEC-01 (light molded pocket instruments, LCDs, orange-red keys). Studio is darker,
rack-mounted, metal and rubber, with color reserved for cables and lamps.

## Tokens

| Name   | Value                           | Role                                    |
| ------ | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Rack   | `oklch(0.25 0.01 255)`          | Rails and the gaps between modules      |
| Panel  | `oklch(0.34 0.012 255)`         | Module faceplates (gunmetal, not black) |
| Legend | `oklch(0.94 0.012 85)`          | Silk-screened text and scales           |
| Rubber | `oklch(0.19 0.006 255)`         | Knob caps, pads                         |
| Lamp   | `oklch(0.82 0.15 72)`           | The key color: lit state, value arcs    |
| Cables | red, blue, green, amber, violet | Which cable is which                    |

**Type.** Saira Semi Condensed. Legends are small and uppercase because that is how
faceplates are printed; readouts use tabular numerals. Body copy stays sentence case.

**Layout.** Modules sit side by side on a rack, each with screws at the corners and its
name at the top. Controls on a grid, jacks along the bottom, cables drape over all of it.

**Principles.**

1. Spend boldness on the cables and the lamps. Panels stay quiet.
2. Every state a person sets lights something: a switch lamp, a step, a knob arc.
3. Depth is a 1px top highlight and a bottom shadow, never a blur haze. Forced colors
   replaces all of it with borders.
4. Sound is mechanical: thocks for pads, detent clicks for knobs, latches for switches.

**Review against generic defaults.** Dark UI with one accent is a common default; here
the panel is mid-dark gunmetal, the lamp color comes from real indicator lamps, and the
five cable colors carry meaning. Uppercase is limited to printed legends.


<!-- docs/phosphor.md -->

# Phosphor: design plan

**Subject.** A monochrome video terminal on a lab bench: a curved glass tube with green
phosphor glyphs, a faint bloom around bright text, scan lines you only notice up close,
a block cursor, and boxes drawn with line characters. **Audience.** Developers building
developer tools: CLIs in the browser, infrastructure consoles, logs, agents, and anyone
who wants their app to feel like a terminal. **Job.** The skin that makes developers
share a screenshot, and the natural partner of the Terminal kit.

Named Phosphor, not Terminal, so the skin never gets confused with the Terminal kit.

## Tokens

| Name    | Value                     | Role                                                      |
| ------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tube    | `oklch(0.26 0.035 155)`   | The glass: a dark green-grey, never black                 |
| Raster  | `oklch(0.3 0.04 155)`     | Raised surfaces (popups, cards): a brighter scan area     |
| Dim     | `oklch(0.75 0.11 150)`    | Half-intensity text: secondary text, borders, placeholders |
| Glow    | `oklch(0.88 0.17 148)`    | Full-intensity text and the key color                     |
| Inverse | Glow fill, Tube text      | Selection, the chosen item, solid buttons                 |
| Signals | P3 amber `oklch(0.84 0.15 75)`, P22 red `oklch(0.75 0.16 28)`, P4 white `oklch(0.95 0.02 150)`, P7 blue `oklch(0.8 0.1 230)` | Data series and status, each a real phosphor type |

**Type.** One monospace for everything, because a terminal has one character grid:
"Spline Sans Mono", falling back to the platform's monospace. Body 14px with 1.5 line
height; headings are the same face at a heavier weight, never uppercase.

**Layout.** Everything aligns to the character grid: 0 radius, 1px Dim borders as if
drawn with box characters, spacing in multiples of half a line. Popups are a brighter
raster area with a Glow border, no shadow.

**Principles.**

1. The interface is monochrome. Color is intensity: Dim, Glow, and Inverse video. Only
   data and status use the other phosphors, so they stand out.
2. A chosen thing is drawn in inverse video: the selected day, the active tab, the
   checked switch track, the highlighted menu item, solid buttons.
3. Bright text blooms a little (a tight text-shadow on Glow text only). Scan lines are a
   static, very faint pattern on the background, never on text, and never animated; no
   flicker, no blinking except the text caret.
4. Focus is a 2px Glow outline offset by 2px, unmissable on the dark tube.
5. Sound is the `beep` voice: short square-wave chirps.
6. Forced colors drops bloom and scan lines; reduced transparency drops scan lines.

**Contrast** (computed). Glow on Tube 11.4:1, Dim on Tube 7.2:1, Tube on Glow (inverse)
11.4:1. Dim started at L 0.68 (5.6:1 on the tube); axe found it under 4.5:1 on tinted
surfaces (badges, avatar chips, event blocks), so it went up to L 0.75, which clears 4.5:1
on all of them; red went from 0.72 to 0.75 for the danger badge. Borders in Dim clear 3:1.

**Charts** (validated, `tests/unit/chart-palette.test.ts`): the tube's green, then blue,
P3 amber, P22 red, P4 white, lavender, cyan and pink, each 3:1 or more on the tube;
neighbors CVD ΔE ≥ 9.5 and normal ≥ 17, the first six pairwise CVD ≥ 9.4.

**As shipped.** Inside inverse video, quiet text and chips reverse too (a menu item's
hint, a tab's count). Code uses white for keywords, amber for strings and constants, blue
for functions, Dim for comments; the Terminal kit's ANSI colors are the phosphors.

**Review against generic defaults.** "Near-black with one acid-green accent" is a known
default. Phosphor differs on purpose: the background is a green-grey glass, not near
black; green is not an accent on neutral UI but the only ink, in intensity steps; the
signature is inverse video for selection, which defaults don't do; and the second colors
are named phosphors used only for data. Monospace here is the subject's own type, used
for everything rather than for small labels.


<!-- docs/ink.md -->

# Ink: design plan

**Subject.** An electronic-paper reader: a matte, light grey screen, crisp black type,
greys made of fine dots, and pages that change by redrawing rather than animating.
**Audience.** Reading and writing apps, documentation, note-taking and focus tools, and
products that want the calmest, highest-contrast interface with no motion at all.
**Job.** The first light themed skin, and proof that the system works with no color.

Named Ink, after the medium, rather than any e-reader brand.

## Tokens

| Name   | Value                  | Role                                                        |
| ------ | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Screen | `oklch(0.95 0 0)`      | The paper: a neutral light grey, not white and not cream    |
| Ink    | `oklch(0.2 0 0)`       | Text, borders, solid fills: the only "color"                |
| Grey   | `oklch(0.42 0 0)`      | Secondary text (7.3:1 on Screen)                            |
| Tint   | `oklch(0.88 0 0)`      | Quiet fills: hover, muted surfaces, tracks                  |
| Dots   | a 2px dot screen of Ink on Screen | Mid-grey fills (progress, chart series, range middles) drawn as dither, the way the medium does it |
| Hatch  | 45° lines of Ink       | A second fill texture, for danger and for a second data series |

**Type.** Two faces with distinct jobs. "Literata", a typeface designed for reading on
screens, for headings and long text; "Atkinson Hyperlegible", designed for legibility,
for controls, labels and data. Body 16px; serif text gets 1.6 line height, controls 1.4.

**Layout.** Calm and flat: 1.5px Ink borders on controls, 6px radius, generous padding,
no shadows. Popups are Screen with a 2px Ink border, so they read as a sheet laid on top.

**Principles.**

1. No color, so meaning never depends on it. Status pairs an icon and a word with a fill
   pattern: solid for success, dots for warning, hatch for danger.
2. No motion. Every transition and animation duration is zero, whatever the person's
   motion setting; a change is a redraw.
3. Chosen things are solid Ink with Screen text: the selected day, checked boxes, the
   active segment, solid buttons. Hover is the Tint fill.
4. Focus is a 3px Ink outline offset by 2px.
5. Sound is the `paper` voice, quiet; haptics stay on where the device has them.
6. Forced colors maps straight across, since the skin already avoids color.

**Contrast** (computed). Ink on Screen 15.6:1, Grey on Screen 7.3:1 and on Tint 5.9:1,
Screen on Ink (inverse) 15.6:1; Ink borders clear 3:1 easily.

**Review against generic defaults.** A light skin with a serif risks the "cream paper,
serif display, terracotta accent" default. Ink avoids each part: the screen is a neutral
grey, not warm; there is no accent color at all; the serif is a reading face used for
reading, paired with a legibility face for controls; and greys are dot screens rather
than flat tints. It's flat but not broadsheet: radius stays 6px and there are no
hairline column rules.

**As shipped** (2026-11-15).

- **Data is the one exception to "no color."** The plan drew chart series as dots and
  hatching, but the chart kit fills marks with a color per series and has no patterns, so
  a legend could not show which pattern is which. Charts and calendar events take a muted,
  print-like set instead, like a color e-paper panel: ink, blue, orange, sage, dark red,
  purple, teal, mustard, each 3:1 or more on the screen; neighbors CVD ΔE ≥ 9.8 and
  normal ≥ 16, the first six pairwise (`tests/unit/chart-palette.test.ts`). The interface
  itself stays ink only.
- Body text is 15px (0.9375rem), not 16px: at 16px the denser kits (data grid, IDE,
  scheduler) cramped. Rich text and chat answers get the 1.6 line height.
- Status: solid bars for information and success, dots for warnings, hatching for danger,
  each with its icon and word. A destructive button is framed in a double rule; an invalid
  field has a dashed edge.
- An empty rating star is a screen of dots; a loading skeleton is dots, not a shimmer.
- Code is set in ink and grey. Inside a solid (selected) row, quiet text reverses to a
  light grey.
- No motion is set inside the skin, so it holds whatever the motion setting.



<!-- docs/app-shell.md -->

# App frame and data display

The frame an app's pages sit in, and the small parts most pages show. `AppShell` is a
sidebar layout that collapses to icons with Mod+B, remembers that, and moves into a drawer
on narrow screens. Around it are a page header, breadcrumbs, cards, tables, badges, avatar
groups, figures, lists, alerts, loading states, a stepper, a search field, code blocks and a
copy button. Most are plain HTML in UISet's styles; the ones with behavior use UI SDK:
Drawer, Tooltip, Preferences and shortcuts for the shell, Input for search, `announce` for
copy, Scroll area for tables and code, and Tabs for code tabs.

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/app-shell @uiset/breadcrumbs \
  @uiset/page-header @uiset/card @uiset/badge \
  @uiset/stat @uiset/empty-state @uiset/skeleton \
  @uiset/description-list @uiset/item-list @uiset/alert \
  @uiset/kbd @uiset/spinner @uiset/stepper \
  @uiset/search-field @uiset/copy-button @uiset/table \
  @uiset/avatar-group @uiset/code-block
```

Each is its own item, so add only the ones you use. They share `shell/shell.css`, and the
ones with icons bring `shell/icons.tsx`.

## Parts

| Part                                                  | Item               | What it is                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AppShell`                                            | `app-shell`        | Sidebar, header and content; icons only with Mod+B; a drawer on narrow screens |
| `SidebarNav`, `SidebarGroup`, `SidebarItem`           | `app-shell`        | The sidebar's links, in titled groups, with icons and badges    |
| `Breadcrumbs`                                         | `breadcrumbs`      | Where you are, the last item marked as the current page        |
| `PageHeader`                                          | `page-header`      | The page's heading, a description and actions                  |
| `Card` and its header, title, description, content and footer | `card`     | A bordered block                                                |
| `Badge`                                               | `badge`            | A short status label in five tones                             |
| `Stat`                                                | `stat`             | A figure with its change in words and color, and an optional trend |
| `EmptyState`                                          | `empty-state`      | What to do when there's nothing here yet                       |
| `Skeleton`, `SkeletonText`, `Loading`                 | `skeleton`         | Placeholder shapes, and a region that says "Loading…" once     |
| `DescriptionList`                                     | `description-list` | Terms and their details                                        |
| `ItemList`, `Item`                                    | `item-list`        | Rows with media, a title, a description, meta and actions      |
| `Alert`                                               | `alert`            | An inline message in four tones that names its tone            |
| `Kbd`                                                 | `kbd`              | Keys the way this platform writes them: ⌘K or Ctrl+K           |
| `Spinner`                                             | `spinner`          | A loading indicator that says what's loading                   |
| `Stepper`                                             | `stepper`          | The steps of a flow, the current one marked, later ones locked |
| `SearchField`                                         | `search-field`     | A search box with Clear and a key that focuses it from anywhere |
| `CopyButton`                                          | `copy-button`      | Copies a value, then says Copied                               |
| `Table` and its header, body, footer, rows, heads, cells and caption | `table` | A plain table that scrolls in its own region, keeps its headings and first column in view, and stacks on narrow screens |
| `CountBadge`                                          | `badge`            | A count on the corner of an icon button or avatar              |
| `AvatarGroup`                                         | `avatar-group`     | Avatars overlapping in a row, with a count of the rest         |
| `CodeBlock`, `CodeTabs`, `PackageCommand`             | `code-block`       | Code in its language's colors with copy; tabs of versions; one command per package manager |

## Use

```tsx
import { Icon } from "@/components/ui/shell/icons"

<AppShell
  brand={<a href="/">Acme</a>}
  sidebar={
    <SidebarNav label="Main">
      <SidebarGroup title="Workspace">
        <SidebarItem href="/" icon={<Icon name="home" />} current>Overview</SidebarItem>
        <SidebarItem href="/deploys" icon={<Icon name="branch" />}>Deployments</SidebarItem>
      </SidebarGroup>
    </SidebarNav>
  }
  header={<SearchField label="Search projects" placeholder="Search…" />}
>
  <PageHeader
    above={<Breadcrumbs items={[{ label: "Projects", href: "/" }, { label: "Atlas" }]} />}
    title="Atlas"
    description="Production, Europe. Last deployed 4 minutes ago."
    actions={<Button>Deploy</Button>}
  />
  <Stat
    label="Errors"
    value="0.4%"
    change={{ value: "0.1%", direction: "up", good: false, period: "vs last week" }}
    trend={[0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.4]}
  />
  {deploys.length === 0 && (
    <EmptyState
      title="No deployments yet"
      description="Push to your main branch and the first one shows up here."
      actions={<Button>Connect a repository</Button>}
    />
  )}
</AppShell>
```

### The shell

- `sidebar` is required; `brand` sits above it and `header` across the top. `children` go
  in a `<main>`; pass `contentElement="div"` when your page already has one.
- `label` ("Navigation") names the sidebar, and titles the drawer when there's no `brand`.
- When the viewport is `narrowBelow` ("48rem") wide or less, the sidebar moves into a
  drawer opened by Open navigation in the header. On the server the shell renders the
  wide layout.
- Expanded or collapsed is saved in `localStorage` under `uiset-sidebar` with UI SDK's
  preferences, and shown as `data-sidebar` on a wrapper. Every shell on the same origin
  shares it, the web element included.
- `SidebarItem` takes `href`, `icon`, `current` (`aria-current="page"`), `badge` and its
  label as text. While the sidebar shows icons only, each link has a tooltip with its
  label. `SidebarGroup`'s `title` names its list; `SidebarNav`'s `label` defaults to
  "Sections".
- `--app-shell-height` (100dvh) sets the shell's height and `--app-shell-pad` the
  content's padding, so a full-bleed page can set it to 0.
- `Icon` takes a `name` from `shell/icon-paths.ts`: `home`, `users`, `orders`, `reports`,
  `settings`, `mail`, `inbox`, `folder`, `file`, `branch`, `star`, `bell` and more.

### Page parts

- `Breadcrumbs` takes `items` (`{ label, href? }`) and `label` ("Breadcrumb"). The last
  item is the current page (`aria-current="page"`) and is never a link.
- `PageHeader` takes `title`, `description`, `actions`, `above` (breadcrumbs, say) and
  `level`: 1 for an `h1` (the default) or 2.
- `Card`, `CardHeader`, `CardDescription`, `CardContent` and `CardFooter` take a `div`'s
  props (a `p`'s for the description). `CardTitle` takes `level` (2, 3 or 4; `h3` by
  default), `className` and `children` only.
- `EmptyState` takes `title`, `description`, `actions`, `icon` (a shell icon name,
  `inbox` by default, or `null`) and `level` (2, 3 or 4; `h2` by default).
- `Stepper` takes `steps` (`{ value, label, description? }`), `value`, `onValueChange`,
  `label` ("Progress") and `linear` (on). Steps before the current one show a check and
  read "(done)"; the current one has `aria-current="step"`; with `linear`, later steps
  are disabled. A `value` that isn't in `steps` marks the first one. The stepper doesn't
  move by itself: your Back and Continue set `value`.

### Data display

- `Badge` takes `tone` (`neutral` by default, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`) and
  a `span`'s props. The tone is color only, so the words you pass carry the meaning.
- `Stat` takes `label`, `value` and `description`. `change` is `{ value, direction, good?,
  period? }`: an arrow plus "Up" or "Down" for screen readers. A rise shows as good and a
  fall as bad; `good` overrides that (`good: false` for errors going up). `trend` (numbers
  oldest first, `null` for a gap) draws a sparkline named for where the values went
  ("Errors trend: from 0.2 to 0.4, low 0.2, high 0.4"), and `format` formats them.
- `DescriptionList` takes `items` (`{ term, details }`) and `layout`: `"columns"` (the
  default) or `"stacked"`.
- `ItemList` takes a `label`, which names the list. Each `Item` takes `title` (a link with
  `href`), `media`, `description`, `meta` and `actions`.
- `Alert` takes `tone` (`info` by default, `success`, `warning`, `danger`), `title`, its
  text as children, `actions` and `onDismiss`, which adds Dismiss. Screen readers hear the
  tone before the title ("Warning: Card expires soon"); an alert with no `title` doesn't
  say it.
- An `Alert` is static by default. `live` makes it a polite `role="status"`; `urgent`
  makes it `role="alert"`, for a message that appears in response to something and must
  interrupt.
- `Kbd` takes `keys` in UI SDK's shortcut form (`"mod+k"`) and shows ⌘K on Apple devices
  and Ctrl+K elsewhere.
- `Spinner` takes `label` ("Loading"), read by screen readers as a status, and `size`
  ("1rem").
- `Skeleton` takes `width`, `height` ("1rem") and `radius`; `SkeletonText` takes `lines`
  (3), the last one shorter. Both are hidden from screen readers. Wrap what's loading in
  `Loading` (`loading`, `label` "Loading…"): it's `aria-busy` while loading and says the
  label once. With reduced motion, skeletons and spinners stop moving.
- `SearchField` takes UI SDK Input's props (`value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange`,
  `placeholder`, `name`) plus `label` ("Search") and `shortcut` ("/", or `null` for none).
  The key shows as a hint until there's text; then Clear empties the field and keeps
  focus there.
- `CopyButton` takes `value`, `label` ("Copy") and `copiedLabel` ("Copied"). It writes
  `value` to the clipboard, announces `copiedLabel`, and shows it with a check for 1.6
  seconds. If the clipboard refuses, nothing changes on screen.
- `CountBadge` wraps a button or an avatar and takes `count`, `max` (99: above it the
  badge reads "99+"), `showZero` and `dot`, a dot with no number. It shows nothing at zero.
  People see the number; screen readers and agents don't read it, so say the count in the
  control's own name ("Notifications, 3 unread"). For something with no name to put it in,
  pass `label` ("5 new messages"), which is read after it.
- `AvatarGroup` takes `label`, which names the group, and avatars as children. `max` shows
  that many and then "+2", read as "2 more"; `moreLabel` changes those words. `total` is
  how many there are in all, when you render only the first few.

### Table

```tsx
<Table label="Invoices" stack stickyHeader maxHeight="20rem">
  <TableHeader>
    <TableRow>
      <TableHead>Invoice</TableHead>
      <TableHead>Customer</TableHead>
      <TableHead align="end">Amount</TableHead>
    </TableRow>
  </TableHeader>
  <TableBody>
    {invoices.map((invoice) => (
      <TableRow key={invoice.id}>
        <TableHead scope="row">{invoice.id}</TableHead>
        <TableCell>{invoice.customer}</TableCell>
        <TableCell align="end">{invoice.amount}</TableCell>
      </TableRow>
    ))}
  </TableBody>
</Table>
```

- `Table` is a real `<table>` inside a UI SDK scroll area. `label` is required and names
  the scrolling region. The region is a tab stop only while something in it scrolls, so
  keyboard users can scroll it and nobody tabs to a table that fits.
- `stickyHeader` keeps the headings in view while the body scrolls; give the table a
  `maxHeight`. `stickyColumn` keeps each row's first cell in view while the rest scrolls
  sideways, and `minWidth` is the narrowest the table gets before it does.
- With `stack`, below 30rem of its own width each row becomes a block, with every column's
  heading beside its value. The headings are copied from the header row; a `TableCell`'s
  `label` replaces one. The table keeps its roles there, so screen readers still read it
  as a table.
- `TableHead` is a column heading, or a row heading with `scope="row"`. It and `TableCell`
  take `align` (`start`, `center` or `end`). `TableCaption` shows under the table.
- Sticky cells paint `--table-background` (the page color) over the rows passing under
  them. Set it on the table when it sits on another surface, like a card.
- This is a table for reading. For sorting, filters, selection and editing, use the
  [data grid](./data-grid.md).

### Code

```tsx
<PackageCommand install="@uiset/web @ui-sdk/web" />

<CodeBlock code={source} language="tsx" title="app.tsx" lineNumbers highlight={[4]} />

<CodeTabs
  label="Framework"
  items={[
    { value: "react", label: "React", language: "tsx", code: reactSource },
    { value: "web", label: "Web Components", language: "html", code: htmlSource },
  ]}
/>
```

- `CodeBlock` takes `code`, `language` (a shiki language, like `tsx` or `bash`; leave it
  out for plain text) and `title`, shown above the code with the Copy button. `lineNumbers`
  numbers the lines and `highlight` marks some, counted from 1. Neither is part of the text
  that's selected or copied. `wrap` wraps long lines, `maxHeight` makes tall code scroll,
  and `copy={false}` leaves the button out.
- Colors come from shiki, loaded the first time a block needs it; the code shows plain
  until then. Each skin sets the colors, and they hold 4.5:1 in every one.
- `CodeTabs` takes a `label` for its row of tabs and `items` (`{ value, label, code,
  language }`), with `value` and `onValueChange` or `defaultValue`. Copy copies the tab
  that shows.
- `PackageCommand` takes `install` (packages to add, with `dev` for a dev dependency) or
  `run` (a package's command), and writes it for npm, pnpm, yarn and bun. The tab someone
  picks is picked in every `PackageCommand` on the page and saved in `localStorage` under
  `uiset-package-manager`. `packageCommands()` returns the same four as `CodeTabs` items.
- Code that runs wide scrolls inside its box, which is then a tab stop.

## Keys

| Keys                     | Where        | Does                                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mod+B                    | anywhere     | Collapse the sidebar to icons, or expand it (wide screens only) |
| "/" (the `shortcut`)     | anywhere     | Focus the search field, except while typing in another field |
| Escape                   | drawer       | Close the navigation drawer                                |
| Tab, Enter, Space        | stepper      | Each step is a button; locked steps are skipped            |
| Left, Right, Home, End   | code tabs    | Move between the tabs, which shows that tab's code         |
| Arrows, Page Up, Page Down | a table or code that scrolls | Scroll it, once focus is on it            |

The sidebar toggle and the search field carry `aria-keyshortcuts` for their keys.

## For agents

Most of these parts are plain HTML, so the bridge doesn't list them: Breadcrumbs,
PageHeader, Card, Badge, CountBadge, Stat, EmptyState, Skeleton, Loading, DescriptionList,
ItemList, Kbd and Spinner. The buttons, links and fields you put in them are listed, by their own
names. Inside an `Item`, a control carries the row's text ("Ada Lovelace ada@acme.dev
Owner"), so when two rows each have a Remove button, the bridge's error lists both with
their rows and the agent picks one by ref.

- **Shell:** the toggle is a button named "Collapse sidebar" or "Expand sidebar". On a
  narrow screen the drawer is "Open navigation", with `setOpen`. Each `SidebarItem` is a
  tooltip named by its link text, with `press` (follows the link) and `setOpen`. A
  `badge`'s text runs into that name with no space ("Deployments3").
- **SearchField:** one input named by `label`, with `setValue` and `clear`. Its Clear
  button is `data-agent-hidden`, so agents don't see a second control.
- **Stepper:** each step is a button named by its text, "Account (done)" for a done step.
  A description runs into the label ("DetailsName and region"). Locked steps are
  disabled and have no actions.
- **CopyButton:** a button named by its text, which reads `copiedLabel` for 1.6 seconds
  after a press.
- **Alert:** Dismiss is a button named "Dismiss"; with two dismissible alerts on a page, a
  step needs the ref.
- **Table:** listed as a scroll area named by `label`, with no actions. Its cells aren't
  listed; buttons and links you put in them are, by their own names.
- **AvatarGroup:** each avatar is listed by its name, and the count as "2 more".
- **Code:** `CodeBlock`'s Copy is a button named "Copy" and its title ("Copy app.tsx").
  `CodeTabs` is a tabs component named by `label`, with `setValue` and its tabs as items,
  so `PackageCommand` is "Package manager" with npm, pnpm, yarn and bun.

None of these parts asks for confirmation. Put `data-agent-confirm` on destructive
actions you pass in, as on a Delete in a page header.

## Web Components

`<uiset-app-shell>`, `<uiset-page-header>` and `<uiset-empty-state>` are in
[App Shell](./web-components.md#app-shell). `<uiset-search-field>`, `<uiset-copy-button>`
and `<uiset-stepper>` are in [React and the web](./web-components.md#react-and-the-web)
(there, `shortcut=""` turns the key off), and `<uiset-stat>` is with
[Charts](./web-components.md#charts). Badge, alert, card, item and description lists,
breadcrumbs, skeleton, spinner and kbd are classes in `uiset.css`. Table, avatar group,
count badge and code block don't have web versions yet.


<!-- docs/forms.md -->

# Forms: schema form, inline edit and upload

Three things forms need that UI SDK leaves to you. `SchemaForm` draws a whole form from one
definition, steps and review included, and the same definition lets an agent fill it.
`InlineEdit` is text you edit where it shows, on UI SDK's `createInlineEdit`. `Upload` is a
drop zone and a queue of uploads on UI SDK's File input: each file shows its progress and can
be canceled, retried or removed. Fields, selects, checkboxes, date and number inputs are UI
SDK's own components; see [the list](./README.md#ui-sdk-components).

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/schema-form @uiset/inline-edit @uiset/upload
```

## Parts

| Part                                                    | Item          | What it is                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SchemaForm`                                            | `schema-form` | A form drawn from `defineForm`: fields, steps, review, submit     |
| `defineForm`, `validateForm`, `toJSONSchema`            | `schema-form` | The definition, its checks, and its fields as JSON Schema         |
| `formTool`, `registerFormTool`                          | `schema-form` | The form as an agent tool, for a model SDK or the browser's agent |
| `InlineEdit`                                            | `inline-edit` | A value that turns into a field when you press it                 |
| `InlineEditRoot`, `InlineEditPreview`, `InlineEditInput`, `InlineEditSave`, `InlineEditCancel`, `InlineEditError` | `inline-edit` | Its parts, for a layout of your own |
| `Upload`                                                | `upload`      | A drop zone, a Choose files button and the list of uploads        |
| `useUploadQueue`, `UploadRow`, `UploadPreview`          | `upload`      | The queue as a hook and one file's row, for a layout of your own  |
| `createUploadQueue`                                     | `upload`      | The queue with no React in it                                     |

## Schema form

Describe the form once. Its fields draw the form with UISet's controls, check what people
type, and become an agent tool's input:

```tsx
import { defineForm, SchemaForm, type FormValues } from "@/components/ui/schema-form"

const invite = defineForm({
  name: "invite_teammate", // the tool's name
  title: "Invite a teammate",
  description: "They get an email with a link to join the workspace.",
  fields: {
    email: { kind: "email", label: "Email", required: true },
    role: {
      kind: "choice",
      label: "Role",
      display: "radio",
      default: "editor",
      options: [
        { value: "viewer", label: "Viewer" },
        { value: "editor", label: "Editor" },
      ],
    },
    seats: { kind: "number", label: "Seats", min: 1, max: 50, step: 1, default: 1 },
    notify: { kind: "boolean", label: "Email me when they join", display: "switch" },
  },
  steps: [
    { title: "Who", fields: ["email"] },
    { title: "Access", fields: ["role", "seats", "notify"] },
  ],
})

type Invite = FormValues<typeof invite.fields> // { email: string; role: "viewer" | "editor" | null; … }

<SchemaForm
  form={invite}
  labels={{ submit: "Send invite" }}
  confirm="Sends an invite email to the address given"
  doneMessage="Invite sent."
  onSubmit={async (values) => {
    const response = await sendInvite(values)
    if (response.status === 409) return { email: "They're already in this workspace." }
  }}
/>
```

- **Kinds:** `text`, `email`, `url`, `tel`, `textarea`, `number`, `choice` (a select, or
  radios with `display: "radio"`), `boolean` (a checkbox, or a switch) and `date` (an ISO
  date). Each takes `label`, `description`, `required`, `placeholder` and `default`, and the
  checks its kind has: `min` and `max` (length, value or date), `step` (1 for whole numbers),
  `pattern` with `patternMessage`, and `validate(value, values)` for a rule of your own.
- **Rules across fields:** pass any Standard Schema as `schema` (zod, valibot, arktype and
  others implement it). It runs on submit once every field passes; an issue goes under the
  field its path names, or above the actions.
- **When problems show:** leaving a field shows what's wrong with what was typed; an empty
  required field waits for Next or Submit. Those check the step, or everything, and move
  focus to the first problem. A field showing a problem is checked again as it changes.
- **Steps:** every field is in one step. Next checks the step, and so does Enter in any
  of its fields; the steps above the form go back to any step done; the last Next shows a
  review of every value with an Edit per step, and Submit sends. When a step change takes
  away what had focus (the field you pressed Enter in, Back on the first step, an Edit),
  focus goes to the new step's first field, or to the submit on the review.
- **`onSubmit`** gets the values. Return problems by field (`{ email: "…" }`), or under
  `form` for the whole form, and they show where they belong, on their step, with focus on
  the first. A thrown error shows under `form`. `doneMessage` is said and shown once it's sent.
- **Controlled or not:** `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange`, and `step`,
  `defaultStep`, `onStepChange`, as every UI SDK component.
- **Words:** `labels` (Next, Back, Submit, the review's words) and the definition's
  `messages` translate everything it says.

### An agent fills it; a person sends it

The form is one component to an agent, named by its title, with its fields as items and
three actions:

```ts
await agent.act({
  steps: [{ ref: "Invite a teammate", action: "fill", args: [{ Email: "grace@example.com", role: "Editor", seats: "3" }] }],
})
```

- **`fill`** takes values by field name or label, as each field takes them: a number from
  "3", a choice by its value or its label, a switch from "yes". What it can't fill, and
  what it fills but is wrong, shows under the fields and comes back as the step's error, so
  the agent can correct it: `Seats is at most 50. No field "phone". Its fields: Email, Role,
  Seats, …`.
- **`goTo(step)`** shows a step, checking the steps on the way as Next does; the review is
  the step after the last. **`reset`** starts over.
- **The submit needs a person.** The submit button carries `data-agent-confirm` with
  `confirm` (the form's title by default), so an agent's press waits for your bridge's
  `allow` to ask, or fails with "Needs a person". `confirm={false}` lets an agent send it.

### The same definition as a tool

`formTool(form, agent)` is the form as a tool a model calls: its name, a description, the
fields as JSON Schema, and `execute`, which fills the form on the page through your bridge,
so `allow` and the confirmation still apply and the person sees every value land.

```ts
import { jsonSchema, tool } from "ai"
import { formTool, registerFormTool } from "@/components/ui/schema-form"

const invite = formTool(inviteForm, agent) // add { submit: "Send invite" } to press it after filling
const tools = { [invite.name]: tool({ description: invite.description, inputSchema: jsonSchema(invite.inputSchema), execute: invite.execute }) }

// Or for the browser's own agent, over WebMCP, beside UI SDK's registerTools:
const unregister = registerFormTool(inviteForm, agent)
```

`toJSONSchema(form)` gives the schema alone: `required` fields, `enum` for choices (with
their labels in the description), `format` for emails, links and dates, and the limits.

## Inline edit

```tsx
import { InlineEdit } from "@/components/ui/inline-edit"

const [name, setName] = useState("Atlas")

<h1>
  <InlineEdit
    label="Project name"
    value={name}
    onValueChange={setName}
    validate={(text) => (text.trim() ? null : "A project needs a name.")}
  />
</h1>
```

- `label` is required. It names the group, the field, and the value's button ("Edit
  Project name: Atlas").
- `value` with `onValueChange(value, details)` controls it, or `defaultValue` starts it.
  `onValueChange` runs once, when an edit is saved, and not at all when the text didn't
  change. `details.reason` says how it was saved (`enter-key`, `focus-out`, `imperative`)
  and `details.source` is `"agent"` when an agent did it.
- `validate` takes the text and returns what's wrong with it, or nothing. Text that fails
  stays in the field, which is marked invalid and described by the message; the message is
  also read out. It clears as soon as the text changes.
- `placeholder` ("Empty") shows in place of an empty value.
- `disabled` leaves the value readable and reachable by Tab, but it doesn't open.
- `actions` adds Save and Cancel buttons beside the field, for touch screens, where
  there's no Escape key. `editLabel`, `saveLabel` and `cancelLabel` rename the buttons.
- It takes the type around it, so inside a heading you edit a heading. The value and the
  field share one box: nothing moves when editing starts. While editing, it takes the
  width of its row.

The root has `data-editing`, `data-empty`, `data-invalid` and `data-disabled` to style from.

## Upload

`Upload` doesn't know where files go. You give it `upload`, a function that sends one file,
reports progress and resolves when it's stored. It runs when a file is chosen, dropped or
pasted.

```tsx
import { Upload, type Uploader } from "@/components/ui/upload"

const upload: Uploader = (file, { signal, onProgress }) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = new XMLHttpRequest()
    request.open("PUT", `/api/files/${encodeURIComponent(file.name)}`)
    request.upload.onprogress = (event) => onProgress(event.loaded / event.total)
    request.onload = () =>
      request.status < 300
        ? resolve(JSON.parse(request.responseText))
        : reject(new Error(`The server said ${request.status}.`))
    request.onerror = () => reject(new Error("The connection dropped."))
    request.onabort = () => reject(new DOMException("Canceled", "AbortError"))
    signal.addEventListener("abort", () => request.abort())
    request.send(file)
  })

<Upload
  label="Attachments"
  hint="Images or PDF, up to 5 MB each"
  accept="image/*,.pdf"
  maxSize={5_000_000}
  upload={upload}
  onUploaded={(file, result) => attach(result)}
/>
```

- `label` is required. It names the upload and its list of files.
- `upload(file, { signal, onProgress })` returns a promise. Call `onProgress` with how much
  has gone up, from 0 to 1. `signal` aborts when the upload is canceled or its file is
  removed: pass it to `fetch`, or abort your request on it, as above. What the promise
  resolves with is the file's `result`. When it rejects, the error's message is the reason
  the row shows ("Failed: The connection dropped."), so write it for the person reading it.
- `concurrency` (3) is how many files go up at once. The rest wait their turn.
- `accept`, `maxSize`, `maxFiles`, `validate`, `multiple` (on by default), `disabled` and
  the rest of [File input's props](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/components/file-input) pass
  through. Files that fail those checks aren't uploaded: each is listed under the drop zone
  with the reason ("huge.pdf is larger than 5 MB.") until the next change.
- `value` with `onValueChange(files)` controls the files, or `defaultValue` starts with
  some. Every file in the list is uploaded, so start with files only if they still need to
  go up.
- `onUploaded(file, result)` and `onFailed(file, error)` run as each one ends.
  `onItemsChange(items)` runs on every change, with each file's `status` (`queued`,
  `uploading`, `done`, `failed`, `canceled`), `progress`, `error` and `result`.
- `hint` is a line under the prompt. `labels` replaces any of the words shown, and
  `messages` what screen readers hear as files finish, for another language.
- An image shows a small preview; other files show an icon.
- Removing a file stops its upload. Cancel stops it and keeps the row, ready to retry.

Check uploads on your server too: `accept` and `maxSize` are a convenience, not a guard.

### A layout of your own

`useUploadQueue(files, { upload, concurrency, onUploaded, onFailed })` returns `{ queue,
items }`. `items` is each file's state, and `queue` has `retry(file)` and `cancel(file)`.
Render UI SDK's File input parts around it, with `UploadRow` for each file or your own row.
Outside React, `createUploadQueue(() => options)` is the same queue: call `start()`, then
`sync(files)` whenever the files change, and `subscribe(listener)` to hear about it.

## Keys

| Keys                       | Where                 | Does                                                      |
| -------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Enter                      | a schema form's field | Next on a step; Submit on the review or a form with no steps |
| Enter, Space, F2           | an inline edit's value | Start editing, with the text selected                     |
| Enter                      | its field             | Save. Focus goes back to the value                        |
| Escape                     | its field             | Put the text back. Focus goes back to the value           |
| Tab                        | its field             | Save and move on. With text that can't be saved, stay     |
| Up, Down, Home, End        | the list of uploads   | Move between files. The list is one tab stop              |
| Delete, Backspace          | a file                | Remove it, which stops its upload                         |
| Enter                      | a file that failed or was canceled | Send it again                                |

A click outside an inline edit saves it, as Tab does. Save and Cancel, and each upload's
Cancel, Retry and Remove buttons, are for pointers and touch: they stay out of the Tab
order, because the keys above do the same from the field or the row.

## For agents

- **InlineEdit** is listed by its `label`, with `setValue` (saves the text, through
  `validate`: text that fails changes nothing), `startEditing` and `cancel`. A disabled one
  has no actions.
- **Upload** is a file input listed by its `label`, with each row's text as its items
  ("report.pdf 248 kB Uploaded") and `clear`. An agent can't add files: it has none to
  give. Each row's Cancel and Retry are buttons named for the file ("Retry report.pdf"),
  which an agent presses. Each upload's progress bar is listed as "Uploading report.pdf".
  Its Choose files button carries the label too ("Choose files, Attachments"), so an agent
  reading the page can tell two uploads' apart.
- Removing one file is not something an agent can do yet: UI SDK's bridge doesn't offer the
  File input's Remove buttons, and its `removeFile` takes a `File` (reported as
  vercel-labs/ui#782). `clear` removes them all.
- Neither asks for confirmation.

## Web Components

`<uiset-schema-form>`, `<uiset-inline-edit>` and `<uiset-upload>` are in
[Web Components](./web-components.md#content-and-forms), on the same primitives and queue.
The schema form's element takes the same definition, from `@uiset/web`:

```html
<uiset-schema-form id="invite" confirm="Sends an invite email to the address given" done-message="Invite sent."></uiset-schema-form>
```

```ts
import { defineForm, formTool } from "@uiset/web"

const invite = document.querySelector("uiset-schema-form")! // typed by @uiset/web
invite.labels = { submit: "Send invite" }
invite.send = async (values) => {
  const response = await sendInvite(values)
  if (response.status === 409) return { email: "They're already in this workspace." }
}
invite.form = defineForm({ … }) // as above
invite.addEventListener("valuechange", (e) => save(e.detail.value)) // preventDefault() refuses
```

- `send` is React's `onSubmit`: what it returns shows. `value` is live, as a text field's:
  read it after `input`, set it to fill the fields (fields left out go to their defaults;
  setting it fires nothing). Vue's `v-model` works on it.
- `defaultValue` (set it before `form`), `default-step`, `step`, `disabled`, `labels` and
  `locale` are React's props. `heading` is the title's level (2, 3 or 4, or `false`); with `false`, name it with
  `label`. `confirm="false"` lets an agent send it.
- It fires `valuechange` and `stepchange`. `api` has `fill`, `goTo`, `next`, `back`,
  `submit` and `reset`, and agents see the same form React's does. `formTool` and
  `registerFormTool` take the element's `form` and your bridge.


<!-- docs/lists.md -->

# Sortable lists and trees

Lists and trees people put in order. `SortableList` is a ranking, a playlist or a set of
steps: drag an item by its grip, or pick it up with Space and move it with the arrow keys.
It's built on UI SDK's `createReorder`, so every step is read out, and on `createSelection`,
so several items can move together. `SortableTree` is an outline, a page tree or layers:
rows move up and down and sideways to change their level, with what's under them, on UI
SDK's `createTreeReorder`.

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/sortable-list @uiset/sortable-tree
```

## Parts

| Part                                           | Item            | What it is                                                         |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SortableList`                                 | `sortable-list` | A list drawn from `items` that people put in order                 |
| `SortableListRoot`, `SortableListItemPart`     | `sortable-list` | Its parts, for items drawn your own way                            |
| `sortableList`                                 | `sortable-list` | The primitive, for another framework                               |
| `SortableTree`                                 | `sortable-tree` | A tree drawn from nested `items` that people reorder and nest      |
| `SortableTreeRoot`, `SortableTreeRowPart`      | `sortable-tree` | Its parts, for rows drawn your own way                             |
| `sortableTree`, `flatten`, `build`             | `sortable-tree` | The primitive, and nested items to rows and back                   |

## Sortable list

```tsx
import { SortableList } from "@/components/ui/sortable-list"

const features = [
  { value: "search", label: "Faster search" },
  { value: "offline", label: "Offline mode" },
  { value: "export", label: "Export to PDF" },
]
const [order, setOrder] = useState(features.map((f) => f.value))

<SortableList label="Priorities" items={features} value={order} onValueChange={setOrder} numbered />
```

- `label` is required: it names the list for people and agents.
- `items` are `{ value, label, description?, locked? }`. `value` is the key; `label` names
  the item when it's read out.
- `value` with `onValueChange(order, details)` controls the order, as the items' keys, or
  `defaultValue` starts it. Without either, it starts in `items`' order. An item added to
  `items` joins the end; one taken out leaves the order. `details.reason` is `drag`,
  `move-key` or `imperative`.
- `multiple` lets people select several items and move them together. `selected` with
  `onSelectedChange`, or `defaultSelected`, holds the selection. Each item gets a check to
  press, and a dragged selection's copy shows how many it carries.
- `locked` on an item means it can't be picked up or selected, and it shows a lock in place
  of its grip. Other items can still move past it.
- `numbered` shows each item's place, 1 first, updated as an item moves.
- `orientation` is `vertical` (the default), `horizontal` for a row that wraps, like tags,
  or `grid` for tiles. Set it once.
- `renderItem(item, state)` draws an item's face in place of its label and description.
  `state` has `moving`, `dragging`, `selected` and `locked`.
- `help` replaces the instructions read out with the list.

A dragged item's copy follows the pointer while the item itself shows where it will land,
and a list in a scroll area scrolls when the copy nears its edge. On a touch screen, an
item drags from its grip, so a finger elsewhere still scrolls the page.

Items carry `data-moving` while they're picked up, `data-dragging` while a pointer drags
them, and `data-selected`. The list has `data-moving` during a move and `data-orientation`.

## Sortable tree

```tsx
import { SortableTree, type SortableTreeItem } from "@/components/ui/sortable-tree"

const [pages, setPages] = useState<SortableTreeItem[]>([
  { value: "guides", label: "Guides", children: [{ value: "install", label: "Installation" }] },
  { value: "api", label: "API", children: [] },
  { value: "faq", label: "FAQ" },
])

<SortableTree label="Pages" items={pages} onItemsChange={setPages} defaultExpanded={["guides"]} />
```

- `label` is required: it names the tree for people and agents.
- `items` are nested `{ value, label, children?, locked? }`. An item with `children` is a
  branch, even with none yet (`children: []`); only branches hold other items.
- `items` with `onItemsChange(items, details)` controls the tree, or `defaultItems` starts
  it. `onItemsChange` runs once, when a move is dropped, with the items nested again; each
  keeps its own fields. `details` has `key` (what moved), `parent` (its new branch, or `null`
  at the top) and `index` (its place there, from 0), and `reason`.
- `expanded` with `onExpandedChange`, or `defaultExpanded`, holds the open branches. A
  branch something is dropped into opens, so the row stays in view, and a branch a row is
  carried into shows open while it's there.
- A row dropped inside an item that isn't a branch goes back, and the reason is read out;
  while it's carried there, it's marked in the danger tone. `refusedMessage` words that.
- `maxDepth` limits how deep an item and those under it go, from 0. `locked` on an item
  means it can't be picked up.
- `onAction(key)` runs for Enter or a press on an item that isn't a branch, like opening a
  page. Branches open and close instead.
- `icons` adds folder and file icons. `renderItem(item, row)` draws a row's face after its
  arrow; `row` has `depth`, `branch`, `expanded`, `position`, `size`, `moving`, `dragging`
  and `invalid`.

Rows are drawn flat, indented `--sortable-tree-indent` (20px) a level, which is also how far
a drag goes sideways for each level. They carry `data-branch`, `data-moving`,
`data-dragging` and `data-invalid`; each grip shows on hover and focus, and always on a
touch screen, where a row drags from it.

## Keys

| Keys                    | Where                     | Does                                                         |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Up, Down (Left, Right in a row) | a sortable list   | Move between items. The list is one tab stop                 |
| Home, End               | a sortable list           | The first and last item                                      |
| Letters                 | a sortable list           | The next item whose name starts with them                    |
| Space, Enter            | an item                   | Pick it up, or drop it where it is                           |
| Arrows, Home, End       | an item that's picked up  | Move it one place, or to either end                          |
| Escape                  | an item that's picked up  | Put it back where it was                                     |
| Tab                     | an item that's picked up  | Put it back, and move on                                     |
| Shift+Space             | a list with `multiple`    | Select or let go of the item                                 |
