The output is a `log` region in a UI SDK scroll area. Once it scrolls it's a tab stop, so the
keyboard can scroll it, unless it holds links, which Tab reaches instead. A click on it puts
the caret in the prompt unless you were selecting text.

## For agents

`runCommand(command)` and `clear()`. `runCommand` takes one line of plain text: control
characters, which could fake what the person sees echoed, are refused. `query({ within:
"Shell" })` returns the last 50 lines as plain text, keyed by line. Commands can do
anything your app lets them, so gate `runCommand` with the agent bridge's `allow` callback
where that matters. (Your code calls the same thing as `run`; since UI SDK 0.1.0-beta.8 the
bridge reads a `run` action's argument as one of the component's items.)

## Screen readers

The output is a log that reads out new lines, not lines redrawn in place, so a progress
bar is read once. Lines the terminal also announces (Ctrl+C, a completion list) are
hidden from it. A very fast stream still reads every line; summarize long output in your
command if that matters.


<!-- docs/studio-kit.md -->

# Studio

Instruments built from UI SDK behaviors: a knob, a patch bay with cables, a fader, a level
meter and a step sequencer. They make creative and audio tools, and they're the clearest
demo of what a skin does: put them in the Studio skin and they look and sound like a rack.

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/knob @uiset/patch-bay @uiset/fader @uiset/level-meter @uiset/step-sequencer
```

## Parts

| Part                       | Item             | What it is                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Knob`                     | `knob`           | A rotary control, built as a UI SDK primitive: drag, keys, log scales, double-click to reset |
| `PatchBay`, `PatchBayJack` | `patch-bay`      | Jacks and the cables between them, by drag or by keyboard           |
| `Fader`                    | `fader`          | UI SDK's vertical Slider with its label and readout                 |
| `LevelMeter`               | `level-meter`    | UI SDK's Meter drawn as a ladder of lamps                           |
| `StepSequencer`            | `step-sequencer` | A row of steps on UI SDK's ToggleGroup, with downbeats and a playhead |

## Use

```tsx
import { useState } from "react"
import { Fader } from "@/components/ui/fader"
import { Knob } from "@/components/ui/knob"
import { LevelMeter } from "@/components/ui/level-meter"
import { PatchBay, PatchBayJack, type Cable } from "@/components/ui/patch-bay"
import { StepSequencer } from "@/components/ui/step-sequencer"
import { UISet } from "@/components/ui/uiset"

export function Synth() {
  const [cutoff, setCutoff] = useState(900)
  const [cables, setCables] = useState<Cable[]>([])
  const [pattern, setPattern] = useState<string[]>(["1", "5", "9", "13"])
  return (
    <UISet skin="studio" sound>
      <PatchBay aria-label="Patch bay" value={cables} onValueChange={setCables}>
        <Knob
          label="Cutoff"
          min={20}
          max={20000}
          scale="log"
          value={cutoff}
          onValueChange={setCutoff}
          format={(hz) => `${Math.round(hz)} Hz`}
        />
        <PatchBayJack port="lfo:out" label="LFO out" />
        <PatchBayJack port="filter:in" label="Filter in" />
        <Fader label="Master" defaultValue={70} />
        <LevelMeter label="Signal" value={60} />
        <StepSequencer label="Pattern" value={pattern} onValueChange={setPattern} current={4} />
      </PatchBay>
    </UISet>
  )
}
```

- **Knob** takes `value` or `defaultValue`, `min`, `max`, `step`, `largeStep`,
  `scale="linear" | "log"`, `format` (an `Intl.NumberFormat` options object or a
  function) and `locale`. `onValueChange` fires as it turns and `onValueCommit` when it
  settles. `hideLabel` and `hideValue` hide the visible label or readout (the label stays
  the knob's name).
- **PatchBay** owns the cables: `value` or `defaultValue` (`{ from, to }[]`) and
  `onValueChange`. A jack's `port` ends in `:out` or `:in`, and cables run from an out to an
  in. `labels` maps ports to names for agents and descriptions; jacks' labels fill it in.
- **Fader** is a vertical `Slider` with `label`; **LevelMeter** is a `Meter` with `label`
  and `value`.
- **StepSequencer** is a multiple `ToggleGroup`: `value` is the steps that are on, `steps`
  (16 by default), `current` the playhead's index, `stepLabel(step)` each step's name.

## Keys

| Keys                    | Does                                                    |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Arrow keys              | Turn a knob, move a fader, move along the sequencer     |
| Page Up, Page Down      | Turn a knob by its large step                           |
| Home, End               | A knob's minimum or maximum                             |
| Double-click            | Reset a knob                                            |
| Enter on an out jack    | Start a cable; arrows choose an input; Enter plugs it   |
| Space                   | Turn a sequencer step on or off                         |

Every change reads out to screen readers: a knob says its formatted value, a jack says
what it's patched to.

## For agents

Knobs offer `setValue`, `increment`, `decrement` and `reset`; the patch bay offers `plug`,
`unplug` and `clear`, and lists its ports. Faders, meters and the sequencer are UI SDK's
slider, meter and toggle group, with their own actions. The [Kits page](/kits#studio) has
an agent playing the rack from prompts like "make it darker".

## Skin and sound

These work in any skin; the Studio skin draws them as hardware (see
[Studio's design notes](/docs/skins/studio)). With `sound` on the root, turning and
plugging make short mechanical sounds.


<!-- docs/agent-console.md -->

# Agent Console: design plan

## Who it's for

Any team adding an AI assistant that works inside their app (a copilot that fills forms,
changes settings, configures things) rather than one that only chats. That is most SaaS
products in 2026.

## Why it isn't another chat kit

Chat UI is well served: Vercel's AI Elements (~49 components), shadcn's AI Elements and
chat primitives, assistant-ui (13k stars). They render conversations. None of them can
show what an agent did _to the page_, because they don't know the page.

UI SDK's agent bridge does. The Agent Console is the human side of that bridge:

| Need                                        | UI SDK piece                                               | Console part                 |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Approve risky steps in the app, not a popup | `allow` returning a Promise                                | `AgentApprovals`             |
| See every change the agent made             | `createHistory`, `describeEntry`                           | `AgentActivity`              |
| Undo the agent, keep my own edits           | `history.undoSource("agent")`                              | Undo button                  |
| See _where_ it changed something            | `observe` + `elementOf`                                    | `highlightAgent()`           |
| Talk to it                                  | `ScrollArea` (`stickToEnd`), `createInputHistory`, `isComposing` | `AgentThread`, `AgentPrompt` |
| See what it sees                            | `agent.snapshot()`                                         | Page tab                     |
| Plug in any model                           | `agentTools` (snapshot, query, act)                        | `runAgentTool()`             |

The console marks itself `data-agent-hidden`, so an agent can never press its own
**Allow** button.

## Parts

- `createApprovals()`: framework-free. Gives `allow` for `createAgent`, plus a queue the
  UI reads. Steps marked `data-agent-confirm` always wait; a `policy` can ask for more.
  An abort (timeout) clears the card and refuses the step.
- `highlightAgent()`: framework-free. Marks the control an agent just changed with
  `data-agent-touched` for a moment, and scrolls it into view if it's off screen.
- `runAgentTool(agent, name, input)`: routes a model's tool call to the bridge.
- React: `AgentConsole` (header, status, Tabs: Chat · Activity · Page), `AgentThread`,
  `AgentMessage`, `AgentPrompt`, `AgentApprovals`, `AgentActivity`, `AgentSnapshot`.

## Look

It inherits the skin around it, so it matches the app. Structure: a column with a
header (name and a status lamp: Idle, Working…, Waiting for you), tabs, a scrolling body,
approvals pinned above the prompt so a waiting question is never scrolled away.

Approval cards are the one loud element: the agent's own sentence about what the step
does, in quotes, and two buttons named for the outcome ("Allow", "Don't allow").
Activity rows are quiet, sentence-like ("Agent set Visibility to Public"), with a "Show"
button that flashes the control on the page.

## Words

Sentence case, plain verbs. Status: "Idle", "Working…", "Waiting for you". Empty
activity: "Nothing yet. Changes the agent makes show up here, and you can undo them."
Errors say what happened and what to do: "The agent couldn't change Region: it's
disabled. Turn it on or change it yourself."

## Accessibility

- The thread is `role="log"`; new assistant messages are announced politely.
- An approval is announced (`role="status"`), never steals focus from what the person
  is typing, and its buttons are reachable with Tab.
- Highlight uses an outline that survives forced colors, and no motion under
  reduced motion.

## Demo

The gallery uses a small simulated model (pattern matching, no API key) so anyone can
try it. It is labeled as simulated. The bridge, approvals, history, undo and highlight
are all real. [Connect a model](#connect-a-model) shows how to drive the same console with a
real model through `agentTools`.

## Set it up

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/agent-console
```

Create the bridge once, in the browser, before the app renders:

```ts
// agent.ts
import { createAgent } from "@ui-sdk/react/agent"
import { createHistory } from "@ui-sdk/react/history"
import { createApprovals } from "@/components/ui/agent/approvals"
import { highlightAgent } from "@/components/ui/agent/highlight"

export const approvals = createApprovals()
export const agent = createAgent({ allow: approvals.allow })
export const history = createHistory(agent)
highlightAgent()
```

Put the console anywhere, for example in a side panel:

```tsx
<AgentConsole status={status}>
  <AgentThread>
    {messages.map((m) => (
      <AgentMessage key={m.id} from={m.from}>
        {m.text}
      </AgentMessage>
    ))}
  </AgentThread>
  <AgentActivity history={history} />
  <AgentApprovals approvals={approvals} />
  <AgentPrompt running={running} onSend={send} onStop={stop} />
</AgentConsole>
```

Mark anything an agent must not do alone with `data-agent-confirm="<what it does>"`.
The step waits for **Allow** in the console, even when the agent opened a modal first.

## Connect a model

The console doesn't care which model you use. Give the model UI SDK's three tools and run
each tool call in the browser, where the page is:

```ts
import { agentTools, runAgentTool } from "@/components/ui/agent/tools"

// Send agentTools (names, descriptions and JSON Schemas for snapshot, query and act)
// with your request. For each tool call the model makes:
const result = await runAgentTool(agent, call.name, call.input)
// ...and return `result` to the model as the tool result.
```

With the Vercel AI SDK, declare the three tools on your route without an `execute`, so
they run on the client, and answer them in `useChat`'s `onToolCall` with
`runAgentTool(agent, toolCall.toolName, toolCall.input)`. Check the exact hook and field
names against your AI SDK version; this sketch isn't covered by our tests yet.

The bridge's `allow`, `data-agent-confirm`, `data-agent-hidden` and change callbacks
apply to every call, whichever model makes it.


<!-- docs/agent-check.md -->

# Agent readiness check

An agent uses a page by finding each control by its name. `agent-check` checks a page the
way the agent sees it, and scores it: the share of controls an agent can find by a name of
their own. On a UI SDK app it asks the agent bridge itself, in any framework UI SDK serves.
On any other site it reads the page's accessibility tree, as browser agents do. Try both on
[the Agents page](/agents#agent-check): the live check, with and without three mistakes in a
form, and a bookmarklet that checks any page you're on. For a public page, paste its link
into [the checker](/check).

```bash
npx shadcn@latest add @uiset/agent-check
```

## In a test

`expectAgentReady` checks the page and throws, with every problem, when the score is under
`minScore` (100) or an error is found. Use the bridge your app creates:

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react"
import { createAgent } from "@ui-sdk/react/agent"
import { test } from "vitest"
import { expectAgentReady } from "@/components/ui/agent-check/check"
import { ProjectSettings } from "./project-settings"

const agent = createAgent()

test("an agent can find every control on the settings page", async () => {
  render(<ProjectSettings />)
  await expectAgentReady(agent)
})
```

`checkAgentReadiness(agent)` returns the report instead, and `formatAgentReadiness(report)`
writes it as text. `root` (an element or a CSS selector) limits where it looks for controls
agents can't see; the bridge always reports the whole page.

## What it checks

Errors, which lower the score:

- **`unnamed`**: a component the bridge lists has no name, so no step can find it. Give it a
  label part or `aria-label`, or `aria-hidden="true"` if it's decoration.
- **`ambiguous`**: a name finds more than one component, so a step by that name fails. A name
  matches every name holding its words: "Region" finds "Revenue by region". Give each a name
  with a word the others lack. A closed tooltip, menu or dialog takes its trigger's name:
  give a tooltip its own `aria-label`, and a dialog `keepMounted` so its title names it.
- **`unseen`**: a control a person can reach (a native button or field, or an ARIA widget,
  that Tab reaches) isn't a UI SDK component, so agents can't see it. Use the UI SDK part for
  it, or put it inside `data-agent-hidden` if agents shouldn't use it.

Warnings, which don't:

- **`unconfirmed`**: a button whose label starts with a word like Delete, Pay or Deploy has
  no `data-agent-confirm`. Add one saying what it does, if a person should approve it.
- **`overflow`**: the page has more than 100 components, so an agent's snapshot shows 100 and
  it must query for the rest. Fewer components per view (tabs, pages, collapsed sections)
  let it see the whole view at once.

Names are checked with the bridge's own search (`query`), so they match the way a step's do.
Components no step targets, with no actions, like avatars, may share a name. A control is
UI SDK's when it has `data-slot`, which UI SDK puts on every element it binds; inner parts a
component drives itself, out of the Tab order inside it (a grid's row checkboxes), aren't
counted.

The score counts the components the bridge lists and the controls it can't see; errors lower
it and warnings don't. Accept a problem you've decided to keep with `ignore`, and it counts as
fine:

```ts
await expectAgentReady(agent, { ignore: (problem) => problem.kind === "unseen" && problem.control.includes("Legacy export") })
```

## Any page, without a bridge

`checkPageReadiness` reads the page itself: every button, link, field and widget the
accessibility tree has, with the name a browser gives it. It needs nothing from the page, so
it checks a site built with anything. `expectPageReady` is its test helper:

```tsx
import { render } from "@testing-library/react"
import { test } from "vitest"
import { expectPageReady } from "@/components/ui/agent-check/page"
import { Checkout } from "./checkout"

test("an agent reading the checkout page can tell every control apart", () => {
  render(<Checkout />)
  expectPageReady()
})
```

Errors, which lower the score:

- **`unnamed`**: a control with no name. Give it visible text, a label, or `aria-label`.
- **`ambiguous`**: controls of one kind sharing a name, like three "Edit" buttons in a table,
  or two "Read more" links that go to different places. Links into one page count as one
  place, whichever section they open. Radios, tabs, options and menu items only need a name
  of their own within their group, so every question can have its "Yes".
- **`unseen`**: something that looks clickable (a pointer cursor starts on it, or it has an
  `onclick`) but isn't a button or link, so an agent reading the page sees no control there.
  An interactive grid's cells, rows and headers, like a calendar's days, are what agents see
  there; they aren't reported, or scored, since a data grid's cells repeat each other's text.

Names follow the browser's rules closely but not completely: `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`,
a label, the text inside (images by their `alt`, icons by their `title`, hidden parts left
out), then `title` or `placeholder`. `root` and `ignore` work as they do with the bridge, and
`elements: true` adds each problem's elements to the report.

## On a page, with Playwright

`checkPage` runs the check on a real page. On a UI SDK page it reaches the bridge as the
browser's agent would: through the tools the app registers with WebMCP (`registerTools`),
once `captureAgentTools` has run before the page loads, or through a global you name. On any
other page it reads the page. `mode: "bridge"` requires a bridge, and `mode: "page"` reads the
page even where there is one.

```ts
import { expect, test } from "@playwright/test"
import { captureAgentTools, checkPage } from "@/components/ui/agent-check/playwright"
import { formatAgentReadiness } from "@/components/ui/agent-check/check"

test("settings is agent-ready", async ({ page }) => {
  await captureAgentTools(page)
  await page.goto("/settings")
  const report = await checkPage(page) // or checkPage(page, { agent: "agent" }) for window.agent
  expect(report.score, formatAgentReadiness(report)).toBe(100)
})
```

## From the command line

`cli.ts` checks pages by URL in Chromium, any site or yours on localhost, and exits 1 when
one scores under `--min-score` (100):

```bash
npx tsx components/ui/agent-check/cli.ts http://localhost:3000 /settings /billing
```

Paths after the first URL are read against it. It uses a page's UI SDK bridge when it finds
one within a few seconds, and reads the page when not; `--mode bridge` or `--mode page`
chooses. `--agent <global>` names the bridge's global when the app doesn't register WebMCP
tools, `--root <selector>` limits where it looks, `--channel chrome` uses installed Chrome
instead of Playwright's Chromium, and `--json` prints the reports as JSON.

## Paste a link

[uiset.dev/check](/check) runs the same check on any public page: paste its link, and it
loads the page in a browser and shows the report. A link to the report
(`uiset.dev/check?url=example.com`) checks the page again when it opens, and each address's
report is kept for ten minutes. It loads public pages only: an address on a private network,
or anything a page or its redirects reach there, isn't loaded. It skips images, video and
fonts, which don't change what an agent finds, and stops a page that takes over 45 seconds.
For a page on localhost or behind a sign-in, use the bookmarklet.

## The bookmarklet

The Agents page has a bookmarklet: drag it to your bookmarks bar and click it on any page,
including yours on localhost and pages you're signed in to. It asks the page's bridge when
it finds one at `window.agent`, reads the page when not, and draws the report over the page:
choose a problem to outline its elements. It runs in your browser, so nothing leaves it.
In your own app, `showAgentReadiness()` from `@/components/ui/agent-check/overlay` draws the
same report, with your bridge if you pass it (`{ agent }`).

## Limits

- A snapshot lists 100 components and a query returns 100 at most. Past 100 components of
  one kind, the check says how many it couldn't read.
- An exact name doesn't win over a longer one in UI SDK today
  ([vercel-labs/ui#612](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/612)), so "Region" beside
  "Revenue by region" is reported, as a step by "Region" fails.
- `unconfirmed` reads a button's words, so it can't know what a button with other words does.
- Reading a page, `unseen` goes by what looks clickable: a click handler added from script on
  an element with no pointer cursor isn't found. Frames from other sites and closed shadow
  roots aren't read.

## Fixes that come up often

- **A tooltip that repeats its trigger's name.** A closed tooltip takes its trigger's name
  ([vercel-labs/ui#604](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/issues/604)), so the name finds two
  components. Put `data-agent-hidden` on its content: agents read the trigger's name, and
  people and screen readers are unaffected.
- **A field or menu that repeats a component's action.** A grid's search field holds the
  grid's name ("Search orders" beside "Orders"). When the component offers the same action
  (`filter`), hide the field from agents with `data-agent-hidden`; they use the action.
- **A row's controls.** Give each a verb of its own ("Open Launch plan", "More for Launch
  plan"), so none is the bare title that finds both.
- **Web Components named on an inner part.** The web bridge reads a component's name from
  its root element: put the `aria-label` of a `ui-tabs-list`, a `ui-scroll-area-viewport` or a
  `ui-slider-thumb` on `ui-tabs`, `ui-scroll-area` or `ui-slider` too.
